en: The Sātvata Tantra,
the first chapter;
the venerable Sūta said:
I take refuge in Him who, though one, becomes manifold at the beginning of creation, O Kṛṣṇa; He who is the embodiment of supreme bliss,
Śiva, the supreme bestower of auspiciousness, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa.
Nārada, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings, questioned him:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear of the various playful incarnations (*līlātanu*) of the immeasurable and all-pervading Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose deeds are wonderful."
For what purpose, of what nature, at what time, and in what manner the Blessed One, established in his own state, assumes [an incarnation]— you should explain that to me,
as well as the cause for his descent and the subsequent manifestation of a physical form after a long interval.
"First, speak according to reality, you who are the best among those who know the higher and the lower.
Śrī Śiva said:
"O illustrious one, O best of devotees, you have asked well."
O Great-minded One, since I was urged to correctly describe the heroism of the Blessed One,
I do not see an end even in hundreds of years to the narration of the incarnations of Śrī Viṣṇu and of Virāj.
Nevertheless, O Nārada, having extracted the essence, I shall describe it in the form of a tantra exactly as it was spoken by the compassionate Lord,
after first offering salutations with the word "Jaya" to the Lord who has assumed the form of a cowherd.
I shall proclaim the work known as the *Sātvata-tantra*, which increases devotion to the Blessed One.
That which was once the single, unmanifest, eternal, conscious, and imperishable—
whom the wise know as Brahman and the Sātvatas call the Blessed Lord (*Bhagavān*).
Then, considering itself as if non-existent without the object of perception, the all-pervading Lord, having himself become existence,
manifested in two ways as reality: namely,
as the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), and as *prakṛti*, *puruṣa*, and the Great One (*mahat*).
The Blessed One is called the sole abode of all the worlds;
his very power is primordial nature (prakṛti), which takes the form of cause and effect,
and which further differentiates itself by means of the three qualities (guṇas).
Some say that Time is the activity of Hari, which is difficult to fathom;
for it was from the agitation of the three qualities (guṇas) that [the world] became distinct in the past,
and because of it, the individual soul (jīva) undergoes the experience of the fruits of good and evil.
That karma is the cause of great birth, possessing an unmanifest form,
for from it there is always the transformation of all states of being.
Those who know the Vedas call that very thing the subtle form of inherent nature (svabhāva).
This Puruṣa has been described as the manifest Lord, whose body is the Blessed One;
though abiding in time, karma, and inherent nature, he is impelled toward Prakṛti.
Presided over by the Puruṣa, the Goddess Prakṛti consists of the collection of the guṇas.
The principle of Mahat arose, consisting of the functions of cognition and action;
from that, impelled by the divine, the threefold ego (ahaṃkāra) was born,
which they know as Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Tāmasa.
The deities of the mind, the lords of knowledge and action, were born from the *vaikārika* [sattva].
Marut, Keśin, the Directions, Sūrya, and the two Nāsatyas are the movers of knowledge;
Vahni, Indra, Mitra, and Kopa are the removers of karma.
From the King (Rāja), who consists of the grasping of objects through the nature of knowledge and action,
there arise the tongue, the sense of smell, the ear, the eye, and the nose, which are composed of that [quality];
as well as speech, hands, anus, genitals, and movement, which consist of action.
From the *tāmasa* [aspect] arose the five elements and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) respectively.
First, sound was born from the *tāmasa*; from that, space (*nabhas*) came into being.
From space, which has sound as its form, touch arose; from that, the wind (*marut*) was produced.
From that, the Maruts came into being; from the vital energy (tejas) arose the supreme form (rūpa);
from the mere form, taste (rasa) was born, and from that, the pure waters (āpas) came into being.
From the waters, the quality of smell (gandha) was born, and from smell, the earth (bhūmi) was produced.
The principle of Mahat is the ego (ahaṃkāra); sound, touch, and light— these,
along with taste and smell, are all known as modifications of primordial nature (prakṛti),
since they are observed by the wise to arise from the very nature of sound.
Therefore, the primary elements (prakṛtis) know their transformations (vikāras) as modifications;
in space there is the subtle element of sound alone, while in air there is touch accompanied by sound. Likewise, in fire there is form, and in water there is both sound and touch.
For indeed, taste, sound, touch, and form— all these exist in earth.
Since the causal factors are present in their effect according to the rule of inherence,
whatever quality is observed there in excess is seen to that same extent.

O best of the twice-born, know that the principles beginning with Mahat are the forms assumed by the Great Self, the Puruṣa, as his manifestations as effects. Having gathered all these together by the will of the Puruṣa, [she exists].
With their portions, they brought forth Virāj, whose nature is the universe.
Within him is a cavity fifty crores in extent,
surrounded on the outside by these seven [elements], each ten times greater than the preceding.
They say that the house of the Puruṣa itself is where [the principle] entered;
for from him arose the collection of the principles known as "non-human" (nāra), which was entirely insentient and all-pervasive. (SatvT 1.33)

Because his movement (ayana) was therein, he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. Since the Blessed One dwelt within the body of Virāj, which is designated as "the city" (pura), the Supreme Person obtained the name Puruṣa.
When that Blessed Lord, the expansion of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti),
himself entered the stainless [egg] in the form of Nārāyaṇa, then,
having attained consciousness, the body arose after a long time.
That which is denoted by the term "totality" (samaṣṭi) is the substratum of the fourteen worlds;
therein exists all moving and non-moving beings. Brahmā, the creator, is his body during the day; the wise know that Virāj, who consists of the worlds, extends as far as that [day].

They declare that the Lord (bhagavant), who is the abode of all living beings, is the one without affliction, Nārāyaṇa, the divine inner controller (antaryāmin) of that Vairāja Puruṣa known as the individual soul (jīva) possessed of ego-consciousness.
He is the inexhaustible seed and the treasury of thousands of incarnations;
by a portion of whom, joined with the quality of *rajas*, Brahmā was born for the sake of creation,
and Viṣṇu, the lord of the quality of *sattva*, was born to maintain the world during its preservation.
Through *tamas*, the all-pervading Lord became Rudra in form for the purpose of universal reabsorption (*pratisaṃcaraṇa*).
These incarnations of Viṣṇu, consisting of his qualities (*guṇamaya*), are brought about by his actions. Now, listen as I describe to you their partial incarnations (*aṃśāvatāras*).
Marīci, Atri, and Aṅgiras were born as portions of Brahmā;
so too were Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa— the best of the twice-born—
Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, Atharvan, Kardama, and the other lords of progeny.

Their sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons were all of great majesty; they emerged for the sake of creation, endowed with the power of the Blessed One. Through a portion of Viṣṇu, Dharma was manifested as the sacrifice, vast and threefold.
The fourteen Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, are renowned throughout the world.
Their sons, grandsons, and likewise the deities headed by Indra,
who are endowed with portions of Viṣṇu, have been described by me as the protectors of the worlds.
By a portion of Rudra, hundreds of Rudra-gaṇas were born separately;
and hundreds of serpents were born, as well as those who are violent by nature.
These have been described in brief as portions of Rudra characterized by tamas.

The forms assumed by this world-dissolver are terrible in appearance and of a different nature. Now I shall describe to you separately the playful bodies (*līlā-deha*) of Hari—those composed of pure *sattva*, peaceful, and the objects of the world's love; listen.

I bow to that Kṛṣṇa, the one Lord, the infinite, whose nature is Brahman, the Supreme Person who presides over sacrifice; he who, in order to protect the universe once again, his own work, assumed various bodies. Thus ends the first chapter in the Śrī Sāttvatatantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Nārada.
In the *Sātvatatantra*, the second chapter;
the venerable Śiva said:
At the time of the beginning of the Yuga, the Lord, the Master, became manifest in the form named Hayashirsha (the Horse-headed One) in order to protect the Vedas;
having slain the two foremost of the enemies of the gods known as Madhu and Kaitabha, he established the famous [Vedas] that are sought after by the scriptures.
Desiring at first to lead the worlds toward the state of renunciation for the sake of liberation, the Lord appeared in his fourfold form.

He taught the stainless yoga to those of pure intent and personally practiced detachment from worldly enjoyments. Among the gods, the Lord in the form of Nārada indeed bore the pure Pāñcarātra, the yoga of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya-yoga*), which is the dharma spoken by the Blessed One for his distinguished disciples and which bestows supreme liberation. (SatvT 2.2–3)

In the beginning, at the very time ordained by the words of Svāyambhuva for the support of the earth, Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of all, assumed the body of a boar to sustain the world; with the blows of the tips of his tusks, he struck down the son of Diti. Beneath the earth, the immeasurable one known as Śeṣa remained for the ultimate stability of the universe.
In that [lotus], this world shines as if inscribed by the digits [of time], its feet served by the lords of the nāgas and hosts of sages.
Below that sat the Tortoise of vast form, his divine body extending throughout the vessel of the cosmic egg;
there Śeṣa also appears like a mere fine thread, whom Yama, the lord of the ancestors, indeed worships.
Having seen Dhruva, who, though only half his mother’s age, had abandoned her body and was performing intense penance in Madhuvana,

the Blessed One assumed a form consisting of compassion and granted him his own realm— He whom even the ascetics and sages indeed praise. Having beheld Kardama’s penance, the Blessed One appeared for the sake of his prosperity with a pure, divine, and radiant body.
Therefore, he granted him a boon in the form of a son born of his own daughter, and he created a sacred ford with the water of the *ānandabindu*.
In that sacrifice, he himself—the son of Manu’s daughter, the source of oblations, resembling the fire from the friction-sticks of the enemies of the Asuras—was the one who offered the invocation;
O Lord of the Gods, he was the blessing known by the name Suyajña, whose fame is renowned for the task of protecting the three worlds.

And Siddheśvara became the Lord known as Kapila; the son of Śrī Devahūti expounded to her Yoga together with his own Śakti, as well as the pure Sāṃkhya, which is the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious, to those who were turned toward him.
The Lord Ananta, the son of Atri and master of Yoga, became known as Datta and taught his own conduct with equanimity.
Prahlāda, while teaching the sacred narratives to his disciples— the Haihayas, Yadus, and others who were devoted to no other—
related from his teachers that Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the two most excellent of sages, had come into being as the sons of Dharma by Aditi,

the daughter of Dakṣa and wife of Kaśyapa; and that they performed intense austerities, which surpassed even the heat of the king of the gods, for the sake of steadfast assistance, compassion, and purity of body and mind.

From the navel arose the one named Ṛṣabha, whose desires were eternally fulfilled and who was a lord of yoga; he spoke the Dharma to the subjects through his hundred sons, and thereafter he himself practiced that which is followed by the foremost yogins, characterized by the state beyond action (naiṣkarmya). When the qualities of the mind were being manifested by Susanaka and others in the presence of the Creator, the Blessed One, that very Haṃsa, [acted].
With a heart moistened by compassion, she spoke the stainless truth, because of which the discernment between virtue and vice arose among the sages.
(SatvT 2.14) When Vena had died and his pair of arms was being churned by the twice-born, Pṛthu appeared in bodily form.
Quelling the world's hunger, he milked the entire earth for all prosperity and for the sake of all well-being. (SatvT 2.15)
At the sacrifice performed by Dakṣa, which was caused by the power of Śiva, the Lord received an abundant portion of clarified butter offered by Bhṛgu;
there, the eight-armed Lord manifested for the sake of Bhava, and even the praise offered by gods, humans, and others was received by him.
Born in the lineage of Priyavrata as Gaya, the Blessed One spread his noble fame through his body, speech, and mind.
He too, the Lord whose body is sacrifice, assumed the form of Indra and engaged in rivalry, instilling pride in the great ones.
That son of Saṃvatsara, desiring to produce manifold joy for the nights as if from their very first sight,
descended with the beautiful body of Kāmadeva and sported with the Goddess Umā in amorous dalliances.
Seeing the sons of Prācīnabarhiṣ, who had performed intense austerities, the Infinite One (Ananta) appeared with his own tranquil form;
being compassionate, he granted them devotion to his feet while they resided in their homes and bestowed upon them a daughter born from a tree.
In the Svārociṣa Manvantara, the Lord was born as Tuṣitāyā from Dvija-vedaśīrṣa, becoming the most excellent among all upholders of dharma.
The pure celibate disciplines (*brahmacarya*) which even the sages (*ṛṣi*) studied, he practiced directly out of his status as the Teacher of the World.
From that Dharma, in the third *manvantara*, the compassionate Blessed One was born as a son for the sake of the stability of the three worlds—
he who, known as the illustrious Satyasena, a friend to the Lord of the Gods, drove away those wicked yakṣas and rākṣasas.

In the fourth interval, while the king of the lordly elephants was being dragged by a fiercely powerful crocodile in a lake, Hari—upon being addressed as "Nārāyaṇa"—lifted him up from that water; so too did the King of the Gods [rescue] from the waters of the ocean of existence.
O best of the twice-born, the Blessed One was Vaikuṇṭha, and my consort was the goddess named Jayā, who was worthy of him.
The immeasurable Lord caused the vision of Vaikuṇṭha to be manifested during the period of that fifth Manu, as is well known.
But in the sixth interval, the Blessed One, seeing the gods dejected and their bodies afflicted by the curse of the twice-born, became distressed;
then the Lord named Ajita, the son of the king of the Vairājas, suddenly churned the ocean with the gods and asuras.

When the mountain, the best of peaks, had slipped from the hand of Viṣṇu during the churning of the ocean by the gods and asuras, the Lord, suddenly becoming moistened in heart, assumed the wondrous form of a tortoise and supported it; he considered the itching of his limbs to be caused by the turning of the mountain. Then, desiring to perform great works in the milk-ocean, the Lord took a full jar of nectar.

The Lord Dhanvantari, the enjoyer of the sacrifice, indeed became the authoritative teacher of the science of longevity for men. (SatvT 2.26) When the immortals had entered for refuge while the jar filled with nectar was being churned during his own watch, that Lord, whose desires are eternally fulfilled, became Mohinī for the sake of deluding the Asuras and for the cessation of their torment. (SatvT 2.27)

To Satyavrata, who was satisfying the people, the Infallible One (Acyuta), out of great compassion, immediately manifested his fish-form; even in the ocean at the end of the eon, he dwelt there, teaching the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) to the twice-born as they sought refuge in his boat-like form. To destroy the suffering of the three worlds and to protect his devotee, he assumed the form of Narasiṃha, indeed using the tips of his claws—

Having seized the lord of the Asuras by his broad and formidable chest, he tore at that very place with his foreclaws as if it were mere ground. When Bali beheld the three worlds together with their hosts therein, the Blessed One, assuming the form of a dwarf, requested from Bali three measured paces of land; having thus secured them, He made them His own and gave the celestial realm to the sons of Aditi.

As if to manifest his own words, "I follow my devotees," the immeasurable one entered a fissure in the earth; compassionate, he protected the house of Vairocani under the name Gadādhara, destroying [the demon] with his mace. Then, born in the lineage of Bhṛgu after the death of his father, Rāma took up his sharp, great battle-axe.

Having warded off the kṣatriyas and abandoned the surface of the earth, he gave it back to the twice-born and dwelt upon the peak of Mount Mahendra. With his lotus feet served by the gods, he who was born from the ocean of the Solar dynasty as Śrī Rāmacandra, having been led by the lineage of Kuśika for the purpose of destroying the enemies of the gods, broke the great bow of Maheśvara, the Ājagava.
Then, having recognized Rāma as a wise hero born of Bhṛgu’s lineage, and having married Sītā of radiant and fair beauty, he went to his father, the lord of the house;
there, hearing the words of his wife’s kinswomen, he departed for the forest dwelling with his consort.

Having crossed the waters of the Gaṅgā so that his younger brother might follow him, and having left the glorious Citrakūṭa mountain, he—having subdued the wicked Virādha—ran along while wielding his bow.
Having slain the deer known as Mārīca, the enemy of the cruel lord of the asuras, he was then indeed brought to such a state of vision by Sītā, who had been carried off by the Lord of Laṅkā.

He perceived the moon as having fierce rays, the violent wind as a very gentle breeze, and the garland of jasmine and *mallikā* flowers as a mere collection of pure sparks; he regarded song as the flickering of fireflies.
Thus beholding the man devoted to his wife as if mocking him, the bear, whose mind was struck by the arrows of Love, took delight in the hope that she might be his beloved.
Having gone there, he crossed the ocean by building a bridge with his great friend Vālin, the king of the monkeys, leaping joyfully over the waters together with the forest-dwellers.

Having slain hundreds of thousands of *rākṣasa*s and *yakṣa*s, he recovered the stainless Sītā along with her son and younger brother, and the city of Laṅkā was restored to the Lord of Laṅkā by the Blessed One through a blazing fire.
Without displacing the power of the Sun and other deities, he ruled the earth, devoted to all duties through his service to cows, brahmins, and the wise.
He led all his own lords, who were bowed down by overflowing devotion, from their dwelling in the forest to his own perfectly peaceful abode.

His younger brother, named Bharata, possessed of noble intellect and glory, although residing in his own home at Rāma’s command, abandoned it and became one observing the vow of living in the forest; thereafter, indeed, while sporting there, he performed the crushing of ten million *gandharvas*.

His younger brother, the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa, having gone to the forest and consecrated Rāma and Sītā, endured great hardship. Furthermore, at his word, Śatrughna—whose name means "Slayer of Enemies," who possessed vast valor and pure intellect, who crushed the pride of his foes through heroism, and who was compassionate—went to the forest and, casting off his body, attained that same state as the fire for the armies of his enemies. (SatvT 2.40)

The destroyer of the salt-like Daityas among the wretched, a servant of the noble, possessing an equanimous mind toward himself and others, and delightful to the multitude of beings— Mukunda, while instructing the sage named Mārkaṇḍeya on the worlds within his subtle belly,
the abode of Māyā, remained as an immeasurable infant lying within the hollow of a banyan leaf-cup, intent on sucking his own thumb.

For the sake of protecting the immortals who were tormented by the terrible form of Vṛtra in battle, the Blessed One became their first refuge; his fame was sung by Garuḍas and Kinnaras, and he was by nature the destroyer of their great suffering, fear, and grief. Having seen the foremost of the twice-born as ascetics, no larger than the joint of a thumb, their entire bodies like the water in a cow’s footprint;

Out of compassion, [the Lord] protected these devotees of Brahmā who had laughed at Indra, their hands holding fuel for the sacrificial fire, as they approached him for the sake of honoring their guru.
(SatvT 2.44) Having obtained Duṣyanta as his seed from Śakuntalā, the Blessed One, though unborn, became the performer of sacrifices;
astonishing many kings, he personally performed numerous horse-sacrifices and gave immeasurable gifts. (SatvT 2.45)

Seeing all people in the Kali age to be devoid of strength and intelligence, the Primordial God, overcome by compassion, was born from Vasu and Vīrā through Parāśara; with a concentrated mind, he would divide the Vedas. Furthermore, in the lineage of Vṛṣṇi, the Blessed One named Baladeva appeared, because by his power he crushed the exceedingly powerful enemies of the gods.
When the city of the Kuru king, as if struck by the tip of a plowshare, trembled with extreme fear along with its inhabitants,
the blessed Lord Aja was born to the Vṛṣṇi clan, providing happiness to the people who were devoted to his own feet;
he, filled with all powers, will bring about vast fame, being designated as Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Born of his own body in the house of Vasudeva, he will then go to Gokula and,
sporting with various diversions in the form of a child, quickly bring joy to the cows, cowherds, and cowherd women through his clear infant speech and laughter.
At the command of Kaṃsa, he will slay the hosts of enemies of the gods led by Ulūka, and [he will lift] a great mountain for the protection of Vraja.
Holding him like a mushroom for seven days in his left hand, he wiped away the intoxication of the Lord of the Gods.
When the Creator brought him before a cowherd boy along with the cattle, the inconceivable delusion of the wielder of the plow arose;
then, as the Sustainer, he withdrew that [delusion], assuming the form of the cowherd family and removing the various stains of Māyā from the Creator.

In Vṛndāvana, through the playful songs of the cowherd women accompanied by the music of flutes and the fragrance of spring flowers, he shall bestow upon them the swift impulse of the mind-born god of love;
and at night, he shall cause astonishment among the night-stalking demons and sky-dwellers with his assemblies for the great pastimes of amorous play.
When Kaṃsa, along with Balarāma, has been brought to the arena by the son of Śūrasena, he shall swiftly shatter your bow.
Having subdued Cāṇūra and Śūra in battle along with Kaṃsa, and having suddenly slain the elephant Kuvalaya;
having given back the dead son of Sāndīpana as his teacher’s fee, and having killed the Yavana Jarāsandha and Bala;
and having married a hundred wives beginning with the illustrious Rukmiṇī, he begot ten sons by each of them.

Having slain Bhauma along with his hosts, the Primal God went to the excellent king of the celestial trees to give the jeweled earrings belonging to the Mother of the Gods to his beloved; for by uprooting them out of affection, he— the conqueror of the sons of Diti—
would cause even greater immortality to be obtained in battle by the kinsmen of the king from the destruction of Bāṇāsura’s prowess.
Having conquered [his enemies] at the sacrifice of King Yudhiṣṭhira and cast down the exceedingly heavy seed of the marriage, he will strike [the foe];
having demonstrated in the world the supreme worship of the twice-born and the gods, and having shown his own boundless compassion toward his own servants;
having saved King Parīkṣit, who was consumed by a supreme weapon, he will look toward the welfare of Pārtha for the sake of the twice-born.

Having cast away the impurity of the mind dwelling within that which is bound by desire, affection, fear, passion, and family ties, the Giver—whose nature is stainless and whose disposition is utterly pure—manifests His own form. What more can I say of Him who is devoted to His own true nature?
Even the bliss of liberation does not shine forth before those who are solely intent upon the pollen of His lotus feet.
Or what else? Indeed, for those who have entered the ocean of great bliss, there is no fear instilled by the forces of time.

Having proclaimed his own superior fame in the world through asceticism, fire-offerings, vows, and other rites at sacred sites such as the Gaṅgā, he shall destroy the exceedingly exalted Brahmin caste under the pretext of a Brahmin’s curse, and with his body, he will go to his own stainless realm.

Therefore, there shall be a son named Pradyumna, who brings happiness to people and whose qualities correspond to those of the Wide-Striding One (Viṣṇu). With his joyful face and beautiful limbs, he will cause joy for men, like vessels pouring out the water of nectar. There too, Aja will be born as his younger brother, and even Īśvara himself will be born under the name Aniruddha, acting as the one who sets the names into circulation.
Because of the abduction of Uṣā and the destruction of his arm-strength, Bāṇa will become one whose body is pacified by following Śiva.
From Vyāsa, the Blessed One, a yogi in the forest, will proclaim the essence of the Vedas to the people.
This glorious, perfectly peaceful, and stainless [teaching], composed by the Blessed One, brings peace even to the people of the Kali age through faith.

Having attained the descent of a Buddha, the Blessed One, the son of the Jina, at Gayā created a deceptive lure that utterly deludes the intellect through various attractive guises; he composed heretical treatises for the enemies of the gods when the path of his own Veda had become overrun with heretical doctrines and the twice-born were wandering upon an evil path.

In the eighth Manu-era, the protector Śrīsārvabhauma— known as Vedaguṇa, born from the foremost of the twice-born, and the very embodiment of Sarasvatī— will appear as the boat for the Kalki incarnation; he will strike down the host of kings who are like dense darkness, and as the guardian of established Dharma, he will bestow upon Bali the splendor of Indra.

In the period of the ninth Manu, he will act as the protector of the world and the sustainer of its people; having become the boundless Lord accompanied by Śruti and Indra, he will establish the conduct of men and destroy the enemies of the gods.
Having been born in the abode of Viśuci, the son of the King of Brahmins (Bṛhaspati), during the tenth interval, he will be devoted to the work of composing literary compositions.

In the eleventh *manvantara*, the first deity known as Śrī Dharmasētu— the great-grandson of Arthakari— renowned by the name Viśvasena, brought about the destruction of the enemies of the gods through a battle with a multitude of armies.
Having slain the *asuras*, the Blessed Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) bestowed the third abode upon Vidhṛti, the son of the Lord of the Gods.
Born in the Manu-era of the Dviṣaṇ age for the protection of the world from a Brahmin named Sunṛta, who possesses the splendor of his own power,
the Blessed One shall then become renowned as Svadhāman, through whom people in the world attain boundless happiness.
In the thirteenth future age, the primordial god, the Blessed One, shall be born as the son of Devahotra by Bṛhatī.
The Lord of Yoga, the friend of Śakra, the lord of heaven, who through yoga possesses an immeasurable form like the sun;
though the Blessed One is the beginningless God, he was born as the son of a celestial maiden in the sacrificial hall of Satrāyaṇa.
At the end of the interval, he—whose nature is to desire the welfare of the world—will spread out the threads of the expansion of the instruments and actions.
O twice-born one, these pure collections of incarnations of the Blessed One, intended for the welfare of the world, have been described by me;
they are to be fully contemplated through their constituent parts and are manifested by means of knowledge, action, power, meditative absorption, and the rest.
By these playful bodies, the entire universe, including the moving and the unmoving, is eternally protected.
I go for refuge to that Kṛṣṇa, the leader of the universe. (SatvT 2.74,
Sātvatatantra,
third chapter)
Śrī Nārada said:
O Lord, the incarnations of the high-souled Bhagavān Viṣṇu, distinguished by the divisions of his complete portions and parts, have been described; they should be meditated upon by you.
"O All-pervading Lord, explain to us how this [world] can be a portion, a fraction, or a part of the non-conceptual Kṛṣṇa, who is Brahman, the Supreme Self. Śrī Śiva said:
"O Brahmin, you have spoken the truth regarding Kṛṣṇa, the Soul of the Universe:
that in all his incarnations, the distinctions of parts and portions arise spontaneously from himself.
Those who are skillful, wise, and devoted to the Blessed Lord do not describe [these as real divisions]."
Because it is changeless, undecaying, indivisible, and of the nature of Brahman,
[it is not truly manifold]. However, due to the power of knowledge and so forth, and because of the perception of parts within the full [reality],
they speak of a "full" portion consisting of a fraction of a part belonging to the Lord of the World.

Although qualities such as knowledge, vigor, and virtue exist everywhere, nevertheless, they are observed only in certain cases through their effects, and not in all places. Sovereignty, knowledge, righteousness, dispassion, prosperity, and likewise fame—
Through the direct manifestation of these [powers], one is called "Full" (pūrṇa) by the wise.
Even from a slight manifestation of these various parts,
he shines forth as the Blessed One (Bhagavān), who bears the distinctions of the divine attributes (bhaga).
A *aṃśa* would be a fourth part, while a *kalā* is considered a sixteenth;
and a hundredth part is described by poets as *vibhūti*, each separately.
Therefore, [these are the degrees] of knowledge, virtue, dispassion, sovereignty, and prosperity.
O best of the twice-born, hear from me the distinct divisions of Yaśas:
origination and dissolution, knowledge and ignorance, and going and returning;
they say that the knowledge of these, my dear, is the sixfold supreme knowledge.
Truth, purity, compassion, and silence—this is remembered as the fourfold dharma.
Freedom from pride, discernment, and the mastery of the senses;
thus, O auspicious one, has the fourfold dispassion been described.
Aṇimā, laghimā, and likewise mahimā immediately thereafter; prākāmya, prāpti, īśitā, and vaśitā as well—
these are proclaimed as the eight sovereign powers (aiśvaryas) that bring about the fulfillment of desire.
Servants, ministers, friends, kinsmen, sons, grandsons, and wives;
garments, ornaments, treasuries, and the fourfold army;
houses, land, weapons, missiles, and fortresses—these are said to be the forms of prosperity (*śrī*).
The glory of a person arises from both action and qualities.
Action is said to be fourfold, consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
by means of that, the conduct of the divine pastimes and incarnations is most wonderful.
Although the qualities have been proclaimed by the wise to be immeasurable,
I shall nevertheless describe your sixty-two qualities to you in their proper order:
being devoted to Brahman, being a refuge for all, and indeed having affection for devotees.
Generosity, truthfulness to one's word, valor, self-restraint, invincibility,
difficulty of being overcome, being worthy of service, endurance, imperturbability,
independence, detachment, and personal excellence.
Valor, magnanimity, faith, steadfastness,
fortitude, clarity, profundity, humility, virtuous conduct, eloquence, truth,
and auspiciousness; tranquility, self-control, strength, skill, security, joy, and freedom from egoism.
Contentment, straightforwardness, equanimity, mental fortune, learning, and happiness;
renunciation, fearlessness, purification, splendor, skill, and refuge;
fortitude, forbearance, mindfulness, modesty, faith, friendliness, compassion, and exaltation. (SatvT 3.22–3.23)
Peace, nourishment, purity of one's own speech, intellect, knowledge, and self-protection— these, indeed,
are the divisions of the *bhaga* described in their proper sequence.
That in which the manifestation of these resides is proclaimed as the *pūrṇa*.
From the manifestation of a part, a part arises; from a digit (kalā), a digit is said to arise.

From a manifestation of power (vibhūti), a manifestation of power arises; yet this division does not exist by its own nature within the non-conceptual, true reality that is the essence of the Supreme Brahman.

Because the various divisions of the Lord were individually manifested for distinct purposes through the incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— the pure and great-souled Nārāyaṇa— he is therefore called "complete" (sampūrṇa).
Because in the incarnations beginning with Hayagrīva,
the manifestations of the Lord (bhagabheda) shown were indeed fewer than that, they are proclaimed as "parts" (aṃśas).
For Rāma, the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, and Narasiṃha [are such parts].
The incarnations during the Manvantaras, such as the horse-headed one (Hayaśīrṣa) associated with sacrifices and other rites;
likewise, the manifestations beginning with Śukla, the self-possessed Ṛṣabha, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Datta, and in the Kali age, Buddha and Kalki.
The portions of Viṣṇu are proclaimed through the power of knowledge, action, and so forth.
Kumāra, Nārada, Vyāsa, Brahmā, Rāta, and others are the parts;
they are the incarnations of the great-souled Śrī Viṣṇu, endowed with a portion of his knowledge.
Gaya, Pṛthu, and Bharata are considered to be the portions (kalā) endowed with power;

Brahmā and the others are the incarnations of the qualities (guṇāvatāra), while those who are his partial manifestations (aṃśa) are the vibhūtis. Thus, this complete classification of the full portions, parts, and manifestations has been described by me to you.
O best of Brahmins, due to the manifestation of the divisions of the Lord according to his purpose,
there is no difference, O wise one, between Brahmā and Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
nor indeed, O gentle one, between Nārāyaṇa and him who possesses the nature of an incarnation.
Śrī Nārada said:
O Sadāśiva, describe to me the true nature of the incarnations;
is the Supreme Brahman manifest [in them], or is it the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa?
"Is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the world of Vaikuṇṭha, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the single reality among these, or are they each distinct? Śrī Śiva said: 3.37–38.
Listen, O best of those who inherit the Veda, to that supreme secret as I describe it to you, O twice-born one:
the single, eternal, supreme reality is the one who descends in incarnations.
The designations "Śrīkṛṣṇa," "Brahman," and "Puruṣa" are given separately; yet,
just as the light and the orb of the sun exist inseparably,
so too do Śrīkṛṣṇa the Lord, Brahman, and Puruṣa.
Therefore, those who know the Sātvata-tantra, who are established in devotion and are extraordinary,
[worship] the supreme abode called Śrī Kṛṣṇa— the highest, unsurpassed bliss,
whose residence is the world of Vaikuṇṭha, and whose form consists of pure *sattva*.
The Vedāntins, who are established in knowledge and follow the scriptures of knowledge, declare that the eternal truth is served by the host of its own devotees;
they declare the supreme Brahman to be of the nature of light and immutable. (SatvT 3.43–3.44)
It is without hands, feet, eyes, ears, skin, or nose;
it is endowed with all powers, consisting of light, and beyond the reach of speech and mind.
It is pure bliss alone, perfectly purified, the manifestation of consciousness, and the cause of all.
The Traividyas, followers of Hiranyagarbha, [worship] Nārāyaṇa, who is free from affliction,
the thousand-headed god, supreme bliss, the imperishable,
possessed of infinite power, the Puruṣa of all, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Those who regard karma as supreme speak of the cultivation of the states of abiding, arising, and cessation;
[they teach] that which produces all bliss, is peaceful, and enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
Therefore, [this concerns] the god Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā, and Puruṣa.
In reality, O twice-born one, no distinction at all is described even by them;
for just as a single object appears in many ways through various functions and activities,
so too that Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa is perceived as if he were manifold.
Therefore, for this reason as well, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
entered the womb of Devakī in the form of a human being through his divine play (līlā).
Thus, Kṛṣṇa is said to be the cause of all incarnations.
Since he has spontaneously manifested manifold effects such as creation and so forth,
he alone is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) to be worshipped by all the worlds;
for he has assumed human form for the sake of liberation and other goals for the world of men.

Therefore, people always and constantly worship that Lord of liberation, the Supreme Lord, with various forms of devotion and without desire for anything else. O Brahmin, I have thus described to you the incarnations of the Great Soul.
What else shall I speak today, for you are indeed the best of the devotees of the Lord? —
Sātvatatantra,
Chapter Four, verse 55.
Śrī Nārada said:
There is no satiety for me in hearing the nectar of your words concerning Hari—
his supremely auspicious fame which rests upon the accounts of his incarnations.
Nevertheless, having now heard this, I am filled with curiosity.
O Bhagavat Sadāśiva, tell me of the different types of devotion to Viṣṇu that should always be cultivated by men.
"O Lord, by knowing which a person indeed attains directly to equality with Viṣṇu.
Śrī Śiva said:
"Well asked by you, O virtuous one, for this is the most supreme secret."
I have not spoken this to anyone other than a person who is a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata).
As soon as the all-pervading Kṛṣṇa, with a mind pleased by my meditation, spoke to me,
I was then forbidden by that compassionate one from speaking it to those who are not devotees.
Then, bowing my head at his lotus-feet, I said:
"O Blessed One, you ought to instruct your devotees.
Thereupon, the Lord, the refuge of the virtuous, spoke to me with a pleased mind.

Listen, Śiva— may it be well with you— I shall speak of my devotees, the Sātvatas. Know them, O God, to be my devotees who are intent on meditation upon me, who regard me as their very life-breath, who are eager to hear my glory, and who bow down before all the worlds.

"O Śiva, being supremely satisfied with them, I shall explain the different types of devotion along with their means; through that very devotion, one attains perfect success. O Sadāśiva, even whoever it may be, if they remain steadfast in your word,"
With a joyful mind, the different types of devotion along with their means should be explained to him:
"I shall declare this very thing to you— the distinctions of devotion together with their means—
by which one becomes the best of the devotees of the Lord and dear to the Lord through the chanting of His glories."

O best of the twice-born, devotion to Śrī Viṣṇu alone is called "affection" (prīti) by the wise, because it is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), indivisible (akhaṇḍa), and blissful (ānanda). Nevertheless,
it is considered to be threefold through the distinctions of knowledge (jñāna), action (kriyā), and play (līlā).
Listen to them from me in due order, O twice-born one, with full attention.
When the movement of the mind is unwaveringly fixed upon Hari, the inner controller of all, that state—
consisting of knowledge beyond the qualities (nirguṇa)— is indeed directly the most excellent.

The unsurpassed resort for all the senses is Viṣṇu, the Lord of all; it is innate devotion to the Blessed One, born of action, and the harbinger of liberation. Furthermore, that which arises from the utterance of the accounts of Hari’s divine play consists of pure love.
For that [devotion] born from association with the virtuous is always to be grasped, as it is indeed unsurpassed.
O best of beings, listen now in due order to the collection of means for those [forms of devotion],
by relying upon which a person attains devotion to Janārdana.
Through one's own appropriate duty, through dedication to Vāsudeva,
and through a yoga free from violence, [one should worship] the images and other representations of the Blessed One with hearing,
seeing, touching, honoring, praising, and welcoming.
Through detachment from sense objects, through service to one's own guru,

through listening to the scriptures on cessation (nivṛtti), through patience and other virtues toward superiors, through a friendly disposition toward equals, and likewise through compassion toward the lowly; SatvT 4.19–4.20.
Through meditation on the forms of the Blessed One, through hearing and chanting his glories,
and by perceiving the Blessed One in all beings, devotion free from the qualities (nirguṇā bhakti) is described.
Having attained that quality-less devotion, one no longer even regards liberation as a goal.

"That alone is declared to be liberation, which brings about the state of being a devotee of the Blessed One. (4.22) Now, O best of beings, hear the means for devotion to the Bhagavān, which must be practiced with every effort by a wise person. (4.23)
By the instruction of the venerable Guru,
those intent on devotion to the Lord should serve the feet of the Lord with their own faculties according to their function:
the utterance of Hari’s names by speech, and the hearing of His deeds by the two ears.
With the two hands, one should perform service toward images and other representations of the Lord's body;
with the tongue, one should joyfully partake of the food offerings given by the Lord;
and with the nose, one should inhale the fragrance clinging to Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet.
Carrying the remains of the flowers offered to the Lord's body upon one's head,
beholding the devotees of Viṣṇu and others with reverence,
and meditating upon the form of the Lord with the mind, head, and chest.
One should worship Viṣṇu with one’s arms, feet, and so forth, with supreme joy. One should bring all things, such as wealth and other offerings, for the sake of the Lord.
Through these means of one's own, one should constantly serve at the feet of the Blessed One.
When a natural delight arises toward Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, in all the senses, then that true devotion to the Bhāgavata is quickly perfected; indeed,
that is considered the authentic Bhāgavatī bhakti.
O Brahmin, one who is devoted to this [devotion] does not even consider the fourfold aims of human life.
Within that [devotion], all happiness or even something superior is obtained.
Now, O best of the twice-born, hear the cause of devotion consisting of love.
Listen with confidence and a resolute mind,
having attained the company of the virtuous and being devoted to the instruction of the true guru:
[this is] the hearing of the fourfold deeds of the glorious Viṣṇu from the virtuous.
Regarding them, there is the recitation [of their names], as well as the mental contemplation of them;
the verbal grasping of them, and the praising of those who are devoted to them.
If one should be entirely incapable of recitation or even of remembrance, [one should do the following].
But then, O Blessed One, for one who would always perform this daily repetition of the names of the Lord,
being ever and constantly endowed with devotion,
his devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa— honored by the virtuous— will swiftly arise.
Thus, having obtained that which consists of love and having pierced through his own worldly existence,
he quickly attains peace that bestows supreme bliss.
Even though the devotees have obtained the Lord's form, character, qualities, and activities, [they attain this].
Indeed, these [rituals] do not lead to union with the Lord without devotion to Janārdana;
yet, if one who is unconstrained should perform other means for the sake of devotion to another deity,
there would be no fault therein, since service has been rendered to Hari.
However, whatever the person's steadfastness in devotion may be, that alone they shall attain.
There may be a distinction based on the difference in results, but there is no distinction in the means;
this different classification of devotion along with its means has been explained by me separately.

O Brahmin, it has been described in many ways by the great seers as being free from desire, consisting of fruit, eternal, and superior to the bliss of liberation; yet it is also said to be characterized by desire and possessed of attributes.
What more shall I say today? Tell me, O best of the twice-born.
Śrī Nārada said:
O best of gods, you have described to me everything that is to be practiced;
but what here is to be avoided, and that which causes the obstruction of devotion?
"O Mahādeva, tell me— [I am] devoted to service with faith— the primary means that brings about both decline and increase. Śrī Śiva said:
O Great Sage, that which lies outside the means of devotion must be prohibited for those devotees regarding the Supreme Person: namely,
the preoccupation with the bodily continuum and the attachment to sense objects.
"O best of the twice-born, it has been declared that [this] causes the pillarization of devotion for one established in devotion.
In brief, I have explained to you the pillarization through prohibition;
now hear from me about the fault of giving away devotion, which people must avoid in every way."
Violence toward living beings in the path of the Nirguṇa, egoism in the Bhāgavata,
and hatred toward the virtuous in the path of Love— these are destroyers of devotion.
So too are the neglect of all forms of devotion and disrespect for the words of one's own guru.
Even a twice-born who performs devotion with hatred goes to hell.
By perceiving faults, one becomes faulty; in that case, the fruit will be a fault.
Everything performed with a mortal’s [limited] vision is like the bathing of an elephant.
For service to the guru, when constantly honored, is indeed the foremost of all means of accomplishment;
by it, devotion toward the Blessed One will surely and easily arise.
Therefore, with every effort and with reverence for the words of the guru, [one should practice].
All that must indeed be performed which increases devotion to the Blessed One.
By one established in devotion to the Nirguṇa, compassion for all beings must always be practiced,
being fully grounded in the Bhāgavatī [devotion] through body, mind, and speech.
O best of the twice-born, you have been told that for the virtuous, listening with love to the glories of Hari— which consists of pure affection— is the primary perfection of the means;
taking refuge at the feet of Kṛṣṇa is proclaimed as the root of everything.
"Without which devotion flows away like milk from an unbaked clay vessel.
Śrī Nārada said:
"O best of the learned, tell me of taking refuge at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa."
"Without which a person proceeds even while performing devotion and exertion.
Śrī Śiva said:
"Directly [devotion] toward Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, through body, speech, and mind..."
That which is proclaimed as the refuge based on final perfection—O best of the twice-born, this is said by those who know the Vedas to be threefold:
the first, the middle, and the supreme. Listen to them in order, O Sage. (SatvT 4.57–4.58)
That which is established in the intellect as the state of being a protector from sin and the like toward dharma, sacred fords, deities, and so forth,
is remembered as the first kind [of service] performed toward Kṛṣṇa.
[The second is that performed] toward wife, sons, friends, wealth, house, cattle, and the like.
Whatever is performed with the sense of "mine-ness" directed toward Kṛṣṇa is remembered as middling.
Whatever consists of the self’s taking refuge in the body and so forth, as long as it is based on the sense of "self-ness," all that,
when performed at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, is proclaimed as supreme.
Having abandoned the Lord, that which is dependent on Him, and His eternal nature, no other refuge is seen in reality for Him. One who is endowed with this refuge is devoted to the Supreme Person.
He purifies all the worlds by means of Acyuta residing within his heart.
Therefore, for one who has no devotion other than for Viṣṇu, even his own body is not truly dear;
how much less so other manifestations and the like, which consist of supreme bliss?
Śrī Nārada said:
O best of gods, tell me directly the characteristics of devotees;
with a concentrated mind, I shall show them my affection accordingly.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Sage, the characteristics of devotees are directly difficult for ordinary men to discern;
they are to be known only by Vaiṣṇavas, just as the footprints of a snake are known only by another snake.
Nevertheless, O best of sages, since you are a devotee of Viṣṇu, I shall describe to you their essential characteristic which is extraordinary:
they have their minds fixed on me, are free from egoism, and are devoid of the sense of "mine-ness."

Following the scriptures, peaceful, and friends to all embodied beings— when they do not harm anyone, even one who is harming them, then they are liberated, free from the qualities (nirguṇa), and devoted to the Blessed One.
Without service to Hari, they consider nothing to be dear to themselves;
their bodies, homes, and the functions of their senses are entirely devoted to Vāsudeva.
Free from passion, hatred, and the like, they are devoid of pride and humiliation.
Those whose minds are always contented are considered true devotees of the Blessed One (bhāgavata).
They are pure, devoted solely to love for the Truth, and established in sacred learning, fame, and right speech;
they are entirely free from attachment to talk concerning the three aims of life and from the bonds of worldly affection.
Those who act according to the true word, whose minds are eager for the glory of Kṛṣṇa,
who are intent on pleasing Hari, and who bow down to the world— these are the devotees. Indeed, this is the characteristic of devotees described in general.
Now hear the threefold definition of that which is to be known as the Self:
having realized Hari as the Self of all, a man who is full of affection toward all beings,
devoted to service, and free from hatred among people— he is the most excellent of beings.
Even though he knows Viṣṇu to be omnipresent, he feels affection toward Him according to a hierarchy among the superior,
middling, and inferior; for such a person is indeed of middling capacity,
as his devotion is directed toward Hari only in images and the like, but not toward the omnipresent one.
One who has abandoned the killing of living beings is indeed a common Vaiṣṇava;
but he whose natural devotion toward Hari extends to all his senses is proclaimed as a truly great Bhāgavata, the most excellent.

He whose effort toward the senses results in love for Viṣṇu is indeed a Bhāgavata brāhmaṇa; he is declared to be of middling status. He who performs service to Kṛṣṇa with his senses, yet devoid of love—
That ordinary devotee of the Lord who is free from desire and always joyfully recites the accounts of Hari’s divine play—
he indeed is a great Bhāgavata, the most excellent, and a purifier of the world.

That man who, full of devotion, constantly performs the hearing and chanting of Viṣṇu with love every single day, is the middling devotee. He who would perform the hearing and chanting of Hari for even a single watch (three hours) [is likewise a devotee].

One who is free from hatred toward the devotees of Viṣṇu out of affection is called a *prākṛta* (ordinary) devotee. O best of beings, even if other characteristics of another type of devotee are observed by the virtuous,
you should nevertheless recognize that person by observing their ultimate steadfastness.
O best of the twice-born, for those devotees who are established in the Dharma,
practice based on association with them is the supreme cause of their pleasure;
yet this is so even for those who are beyond the qualities (nirguṇa) and are considered Bhāgavatas.
"O illustrious one, I say that affection for them is difficult to achieve.
You must constantly cultivate affection for those who are devoted to hearing and practicing the pastimes of Hari, so that your devotion to Hari does not perish. (SatvT 4.86–87)
Thus, O Brahmin, the characteristics of the virtuous have been described separately;
they bring joy to devotees and are the cause of liberation for people.
O child, the various types of devotion have been defined by me through this practice.

It belongs to all castes, it is pure, and it removes the weariness of all stages of life. It exists at all times, it is eternal, and it bestows the accomplishments of all teachers. It is esteemed throughout the four ages and is the means for accomplishing what is dear to the Blessed One.
In the Sātvata-tantra, the fifth chapter; Śrī Nārada said:
O Preceptor of the Gods, you have described to me the characteristics of devotion to the Blessed One,
which is esteemed in all four ages and brings happiness to the entire world.
Now, O Lord of Devas, speak out of a desire for the welfare of people.

The means to liberation through the service of Śrī Viṣṇu is in accordance with the [respective] Yugas. O Lord of the Gods, please explain in brief the characteristics of the people, the manifestations of Viṣṇu, his various signs, his dharma, and the enumeration of his names.
The venerable Śiva said:
In the Kṛta age, all subjects were pure, free from passion and the like;
they were considered peaceful and possessed of the vision of tranquility through innate yoga.
But for them, O Mahāmati, the meditation on the Blessed One is that which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra;
that alone is the supreme Dharma of that age.
That meditation is said to be threefold, endowed with ten names.

One should perform that supreme meditation, which has no support and yet has a support, and which consists of the internal concentration on all things, endowed with its six limbs until its culmination. O best of beings, first hear about the "supportless" [meditation], which is difficult to grasp.
Non-violence, celibacy, truthfulness, modesty regarding what should not be done,
non-stealing, lack of accumulation, silence, non-attachment, fearlessness, compassion,
steadfastness in dharma, and faith— O best of beings, these are the twelve *yamas*.
The meditator, indeed, being free from sloth, should first perform the first limb, *yama*.
[He should practice] purity of body, purity of mind, recitation, fire-offerings, austerity, vows,
ancestral rites, service to guests, and attendance upon sacred fords that grant great satisfaction.

One should perform service to the teacher with the desire for the sake of others, characterized by the restraint of the two [types of] hatred; this is the second limb of meditation. Now hear from me the third limb:
one should place the tips of the feet against one's own knees, with the shanks positioned alternately between them.
Placing both hands within the lap—that position is known as the seat (āsana).

One should perform the four-limbed breath control (prāṇāyāma) using the mantra *praṇava* alone, through inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*), either in their natural order or in reverse. (SatvT 5.12–13)
The vigilant yogi should perform the fifth [limb], withdrawal (pratyāhāra), by means of the mind withdrawing the senses from their objects into the heart;
this is the supreme limb of meditation, the direct steadiness of the mind through the vital breath (prāṇa).
The yogi, composed in meditation and gazing at the tip of his own nose,
should remain focused with his intellect upon that which consists of light, self-luminous, and beyond the reach of speech and mind, until it becomes manifest.
Practicing thus day after day, the yogi, with his impurities completely purified,
attains after a long time the supreme samādhi, the state of Brahman. O Brahmin, listen now briefly to the meditation on Hari with its remaining stages.
Endowed with that very same method, one should contemplate in the mind as follows:
within the pericarp of the heart-lotus, one should meditate upon Hari, the Puruṣa, whose body is composed of pure sattva, who has four arms, and who resembles pure crystal. (SatvT 5.18–19)
Wearing matted locks and bark garments, with a black antelope skin as his upper cloth,
he bore a rosary, a sacred thread, as well as a staff and a water-pot;
he was a celibate student, eternal, and worthy of worship by those who seek the heart's goal.

His lotus-face has a beautiful nose, beautiful eyebrows, and a handsome forehead; it possesses beautiful teeth and a neck marked with three lines like a conch shell. His four arms are long and extended, graced by hands that resemble tender sprouts.

He has beautiful eyes, a noble heart, and a well-formed belly marked by folds; he possesses a deep navel and auspicious thighs, knees, calves, and feet. His fingers resemble the shape of lovely petals, and his nails possess the radiant luster of the moon.
For one who thus contemplates the form of Viṣṇu, which is enchanting to the world, supreme bliss will quickly arise, and prosperity will swiftly come to pass. Therefore,
this meditation on the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) brings about swift accomplishment.
Listen attentively, O Brahmin, free from the arrogance of pride:
this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is presided over by the form of the Blessed One.
Contemplate this, O twice-born one, with body, speech, and mind devoid of hatred.
O twice-born one, one should honor superiors with devotion, equals with friendship, and inferiors with compassion;
one should treat enemies with indifference while remaining full of mercy.
For one who contemplates in this way, [this leads] until the realization of the Self in all things.
Before long, one shall attain with the mind a mass of supreme bliss.
In the Tretā age, all living beings will be devoted to recitation and fire-offerings;
they will be well-disciplined, living happily, and will be great householders of noble soul.
For them, however, the sacrifice to the Blessed One is the direct means for achieving liberation.
O best of the twice-born, that alone was the supreme dharma in the Tretā age;
therein they worship the Teacher of the World, the embodiment of sacrifice, who has the luster of blood.
Then, through constant and occasional sacrificial sessions (*sattra*), sacrifices performed ten thousand times with the eight names,
and according to the prescriptions of the three Vedas, people attain liberation. But in the Dvāpara age, people are joyful, robust, and capable of performing ritual acts.
Those whose minds are attached to enjoyments are obscured by the nature of pleasure and pain.
For them, worship of the Blessed One is the supreme means for attaining liberation;
that worship is traditionally held to be of two kinds: with its limbs and sub-limbs (*sāṅgopāṅga*), and absolute (*kevala*).
That indeed is the supreme dharma of the Dvāpara age; in that age,
O Great King, men worship the one whose characteristics have been described,
who is yellow in color, with Vedic mantras equal to the twelve names.
In the Kali age, people will be unfortunate, lazy, and beset by suffering;
they will be devoted to their genitals and bellies, petty, wretched, and impure in mind.
For them, a single method has been declared as the direct cause of liberation.
The chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s name brings about all happiness;
for at the beginning of the Kali age, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, descended and spread his pure fame, which removes the impurities of the Kali age.
Having combined all his meditations, yogic practices, and ritual actions, he who was devoted to compassion established them in his own glory and departed for the supreme Vaikuṇṭha;
O dear one, he is the Supreme God, the delighter of Devakī and the gods.
O Brahmin, in that Kali age, those who hear the stainless fame of Hari will for the most part become devotees of Him who is dark like a sapphire and is worshipped through Tantras and Mantras;
therefore, the Kali age is the best of ages.

Therefore, in the Kṛta and subsequent ages, those for whom dharma is supreme desire their own birth in the Kali age as the cause for devotion to the Blessed One. Whatever fruit is obtained by people through meditation, sacrifice, and worship, [is attained here]. (SatvT 5.42–5.43)
In the Kali age, that [merit] which was obtained through rituals such as the *kṛta* is indeed obtained through chanting and other such acts.
No restriction regarding place, time, or performer is prescribed for chanting. Therefore, in the Kali age, the supreme dharma is the excellent chanting of the names of Hari.
For this reason, the wise who dwell through the three ages praise the Kali age,
wherein one attains the supreme state by mere glorification;
whereas those beings who, even in the Kṛta and other ages, were not liberated through their own dharma.
Even they shall attain liberation in the Kali age through mere chanting;
for there is one great virtue in this ocean of the faults of the Kali age:
by the mere chanting of the names, people obtain the fourfold aims of life.

O best of Brahmins, even in the Kṛta and other ages, the chanting of Hari’s name was accomplished through austerities and other means; however, in the Kali age, it has become the means for both [austerities and their fruits]. Therefore, in the Kali Yuga, the chanting of Viṣṇu’s name is supreme.
It is proclaimed that for those established in devotion, the means (*sādhana*) and the goal (*sādhya*) are one and the same:
by constantly chanting the name of Hari with any disposition whatsoever, they abandon sin and attain the supreme state; how much more so for one who recites it with faith?

O best of the twice-born, in the Kali age, those who are solely devoted to the Name are always called great Bhāgavatas, for they perform what is dear to the Blessed One. Therefore, O Brahmin, with your whole being, practice the glorification of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
One who is constantly endowed with faith [attains] this very great fruit. (SatvT 5.53,
Sātvatatantra,
Sixth Chapter)
Śrī Nārada said:
O Lord, you have described to me the chanting of the names of Hari,
which removes sins, bestows great happiness, and is the cause of devotion to the Blessed One.
"In that regard, O best of gods, I desire to know in their entirety those names which I proclaim out of curiosity. Śrī Śiva said:
O twice-born one, even if the atoms of earth, water,
and fire could be counted over many lifetimes, the qualities of Hari cannot be counted;
nevertheless, I shall describe the primary and most wonderful quality of Śrī Viṣṇu.
If indeed this thousand names was spoken to Pārvatī by the Compassionate One—
having seen me established in meditative absorption, the fair-complexioned Pārvatī questioned the supreme god, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World.
Then, for her sake, I proclaimed the Lord of the Universe, who is devoted to me,
along with his thousand names according to his qualities and actions. I shall declare that to you, for you are a great devotee of the Lord.
By the mere remembrance of whom a person may attain perfection—
[him who is] shining like a newly risen cloud, possessing an unimpeded abode, wearing a beautiful yellow garment radiant with fire,
endowed with a crown, rays of light, armlets, and necklaces, and resplendent with a girdle, bracelets, and rings on his fingers.

I remember in my mind Kṛṣṇa, the Ancient Person, whose lotus feet are worshipped by hosts of gods beginning with Brahmā, who is served by Śrī, whose form is the most beautiful of all, and who is cherished by cows, cowherd women, and throngs of sages. Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva, to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.

To the destroyer of the afflictions of those who bow before him, the bestower of supreme bliss— Oṃ! Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Śrī, the Possessor of Śrī, the Bearer of Śrī, the Refuge of the Bliss of Śrī, the Giver of Śrī,
the Maker of Śrī, the Lord of Śrī, the One to be served by Śrī, and the Manifestor of Śrī.
The Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Highest Lord, the Supreme Sovereign,
the Supreme Bliss, the Supreme Abode, the Bestower of Supreme Bliss;
He is without support, changeless, untainted, and unrestrained.
He is eternal bliss, eternally liberated, effortless, and dear to those free from desire.
He speaks kindly, acts kindly, gives kindly, and brings joy to others.
He follows what is pleasing, clings to what is pleasing, possesses a pleasing reputation, and is dearer than the dearest.
He is the great renouncer, the great enjoyer, the great yogi, and the one of great austerity;
he is the Great-Souled One, the best among the great, the great Lord of the worlds, and the Great One himself.
He is the one whose purpose is accomplished, whose resolve is perfected, the giver of success, and the means for attaining perfection.
The Lord of Siddhas, the foremost on the path of the perfected, the sole protector of the world of the Siddhas;
the beloved, the distinguished, the one desired by the learned, the most expansive, the victorious, the supreme;
the eldest, the best, the one desired by all, Viṣṇu, the radiant, the imperishable.
The all-pervading Śambhu, the Lord, the Infinite, self-born, possessing a form of innate bliss;
full of love, the giver of love, the bestower of love, and the increaser of love;
the Lord of Yoga, attainable through Yoga, the Master of Yogins, and one who has reached the further shore of Yoga.
The giver of yoga, the lord of yoga, the one who brings about the accomplishment of yoga;
he whose vow is truth, who is devoted to truth, who is the triple truth, and who is the cause of truth;
he who is the refuge of truth, who takes away what is not true, the protector of the good, and the increaser of truth.

He is all-bliss, the remover of all, the omnipresent, the subduer of all; he is the protector from all, the source of all happiness, and an ocean for the multitude of all sacred scriptures. He is Janārdana, the Lord of the world, the savior of the world, and the father of the world.
The creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, the embodiment of the bliss of the world;
the lord of the earth, the lord of the worlds, the lord of heaven, the lord of all worlds; the lord of knowledge, the lord of wealth, the lord of truth, the lord of Kamalā.
He who is fourfold in nature, four-armed, the bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life,
the fourfold manifestation, the abode of the four, the ordainer of the four ages; the primordial god, the god of gods, the lord of gods, and the sustainer of the gods.
The creator of gods, the sustainer of gods, the god whose lotus feet are praised by the gods;
the Lord of the universe, the one whose form is the universe, the soul of the universe, the one whose face is everywhere;
the progenitor of the universe, the giver of the fruits of the universe, the one who moves through the universe, the leader of the universe.
The creator of beings, the sustainer of beings, existence itself, the self of beings, the progenitor of beings;
the bestower of prosperity, the expansion of beings, manifestation, and the protector of prosperity.
Nārāyaṇa, the one who reclines upon the waters, the progenitor of men, and the life-sustainer of men.
He does not bestow fruit upon others, nor does he grant liberation to others, nor is he the leader of others.
He possesses a thousand forms, a thousand names, and a thousand bodies;
he has a thousand heads and possesses a thousand feet, eyes, arms, and heads.
Padmanābha, Padmagarbha, Padmī,
Padmanibhekṣaṇa, Padmaśāyī, Padmamālī, and he whose two feet are marked with lotuses;
he who is possessed of vigor, stability, eloquence, heroism, fortitude, and patience.
The wise one, devoted to the Dharma, the enjoyer, the Blessed One, the destroyer of fear;
the victorious, the conqueror, the victor, the giver of victory, the increaser of victory;
the immeasurable, the honor-giver, the honorable, the possessor of greatness, the one of great strength.

Contented, bestowing contentment, a giver, self-controlled, compassionate toward the wretched, wise, renowned, steadfast, and a refuge for vigor, energy, and strength; Hayagrīva, of great splendor, who finds delight in the great ocean.
The destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the creator of the Vedas, and the protector of the Vedas;
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana;
he who maintains the unbroken vow of Brahman, the Self, and the discerning teacher of yoga.
The illustrious Nārada is a divine seer who initiates both action and inaction;
he is the author of the Sātvata Āgama and the indicator of what is beneficial and harmful for the world.
He is the primordial time, the essence of sacrifice, and was born from the nostril of the Creator.
He who holds the terrestrial globe upon the tips of his teeth, the destroyer of Hiraṇyākṣa’s army,
the lord of the earth, possessed of swift speed, with the oceans contained within the pores of his skin,
who shook Mount Meru with his breath, and is praised by the Lord of Progenitors.
Ananta, the supporter of the earth, who dwells in the depths of Pātāla;
swift as the fire of desire, the king of the serpent kings, possessed of great splendor;
the Great Tortoise, whose body is the universe, the bearer of Śeṣa, and the protector of all.
The sovereign lord of the hosts of world-fathers, whose great state is praised by the fathers;
he who consists of compassion, the self-manifested one, who increases the constant joy [of his devotees];
whose feet are praised by Dhruva, the bestower of the realm of Viṣṇu, worshipped by the worlds.
He is white, scorched by the mud [of worldly existence], his mind satisfied through austerity;
he is the granter of the heart's desires, a lake adorned with drops of joy;
he is the sacrifice, the sovereign of the hosts of gods, and the slayer of Daityas and Dānavas.
The protector of Manu, the guardian of the world, the one who brought about the birth of the world-protectors;
he named Kapila, the founder of Sāṃkhya, born from the body of Kardama;
the sovereign lord of all the hosts of Siddhas, the one who granted the final goal to Devahūtī.
Datta, the son of Atri, is a yogi who reveals the path of yoga;
he brings joy to Anasūyā and is praised by all practitioners of yoga.
Nārāyaṇa, the sage Nara, the son of Dharma, is high-minded.
The subduer of Maheśa’s trident, the sole bestower of boons upon Maheśa;
steadfast in penance until the end of the kalpa, the remover of the intoxication of Manmatha and others;
he who conquered the bodiless one (Anaṅga) through Urvaśī, and the giver of what is dear to Mārkaṇḍeya.
He who grants the heart's desire to the Ṛbhus, the beloved son of Merudevī,
the creator of the king of yogis and the twice-born, the demonstrator of the practice of yoga,
the eight-armed one, the purifier of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, and the one honored by all.
The subduer of Dakṣa’s hatred, the bestower of knowledge upon Dakṣa,
born in the lineage of Priyavrata, he was named Gaya, possessed of great fame,
noble in his deeds, highly learned, and an ocean of a multitude of great virtues.
In the form of a swan, he is the speaker of reality, the discriminator between virtue and vice,
the quencher of the Creator’s shame, and beloved by those who practice celibacy. As the Vaiśya Pṛthu, he is the milker of the earth, performing the milking that provides life for all beings.
The first king, the builder of human dwellings and the leveler of the earth;
his station praised by Pracetas, he of peaceful form and beautiful appearance;
the lord of the hosts of day and night, possessing a banner, the refuge of the unborn.
Śrī Kāmadeva, who performs the playful pastimes of love with Kamalā;
he who grants delight at his own feet, bestows desired happiness, and destroys suffering;
the all-pervading Lord, the foremost among the upholders of Dharma, the head of the Vedas, and the son of the twice-born.
The giver of instruction to eighty-eight thousand sages;
Satyasena, the burner of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, the protector of the distressed;
Indramitra, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, who delights in the Dharma of truthful speech.
Hari is the protector of the noble elephant, the destroyer of the crocodile’s noose,

the one who praises the forests of Mount Trikūṭa, and the seeker of the welfare of all worlds. He is Vaikuṇṭha, the bestower of auspiciousness and freedom from suffering, the son of the beautiful lady of Vikuṇṭha.
The beloved of Ramā, the illustrious one, the revealer of his own realm;
the remover of the suffering of the gods distressed by the Brahmin’s curse;
the churner of the ocean of milk, the Brahmin, the unconquered son of Virāja.
The upholder of Mount Mandara, the Tortoise who grants welfare to gods and demons,
the Creator equal to Jambūdvīpa, and the cause of the production of nectar;
Dhanvantari, the healer of disease, the milker of immortality, and the pacifier of ailments.
The author of Āyurveda, the king of physicians, the bestower of knowledge;
the one who grants fearlessness to the gods, the deluder of the Daityas, she who assumes forms at will;
the drinker of the nectar of the immortals, the deceiver of the wicked Daityas and Dānavas.
The great fish of vast body, within whose scales lies the ocean;

the subduer of the Veda-enemy Daityas and the protector of the rice seed; he who causes the sea to swirl with the stroke of his tail and bestows that which is dear to those devoted to the vow of truth.
The protector of his devotees and of the vow of truth, the one who reveals the threefold yoga;
Narasiṃha, whose tongue is the world, with spike-like ears and claws as weapons;
he who shakes the clouds with his mane and surpasses all radiance with the luster of his teeth.
The destroyer of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the subduer of the pride of many dānavas,
whose lotus feet are praised by the gods, who removes the suffering of saṃsāra for his devotees,
the slayer of the fear of Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra, and the accomplisher of the work of the gods.
Resembling a blazing fire, he is the destroyer of all fears;
the shatterer of great impurities, the bestower of boons for all desires;
the annihilator through the prowess of Time, and the remover of the afflictions caused by the planets.
He is the pacifier of all diseases and the wielder of the staff against fierce enemies;
he wards off the suffering of Hara when terrified by the fierce Bhairava.
His head is covered with the skin of Brahmā, and he wears the head of Śiva as his sole anklet.
The single jewel upon the heads of the twelve Ādityas, adorned by the guardians of the quarters;
Vāmana, the destroyer of Aditi’s fear, the ornament of the assembly of the twice-born;
he who obtained the wealth of the three worlds through the pretext of begging for three paces.

He who has cracked the shell of the universe with his claws, whose valor is immeasurable, who is the progenitor of the sacred ford of the celestial river (Ganges), who is worshiped by Brahmā, and who removes all fear; he who destroys the flood of sins with the water from his own feet, and who is the singular vision of the universal form.
He who makes offerings dear to him, the devotee, the milker of heaven,
the wielder of the mace; the son of Jamadagni, possessed of great heroism, the bearer of the axe, the conqueror of Kārtavīrya, the destroyer of Sahasrārjuna, and the ender of all kṣatriya lineages.
He who makes the earth free of kṣatriyas, the conqueror of heroes, the bestower of sovereignty upon the brahmins;
he who proclaims the Veda of Droṇa’s weapons, and the giver of fame to the teacher Maheśa;
he who is the sun that causes the lotus of the solar dynasty to bloom, the son of the illustrious Daśaratha.
Śrī Rāma, Rāmacandra, Rāmabhadra, and Amitaprabha;
he who resembles the color of sapphire, the life-breath of Kausalyā,
lotus-eyed, lotus-faced, and whose lotus-feet are marked with lotuses.
With long arms and beautiful limbs, adorned with jewel ornaments,
wearing celestial garments and wielding a divine bow, he has mastered the divine weapons bestowed upon him;
with sword in hand, he is the lord of heroes, possessed of immeasurable prowess.
The preceptor of Viśvāmitra, a bowman and the foremost among those learned in the science of archery; he who struck down Tāḍaka with a multitude of blows for the sake of the straight path;
Subāhu, rich in the prowess of his arms and the slayer of many Rākṣasas.
He who achieved the breaking of the fierce bow of Caṇḍīśa’s mighty arm;
the one who generates joy for Janaka; the beloved leader of Jānakī;
the destroyer of the pride of the host of enemies; and the one who eclipsed the prowess of Bhārgava.
His mind fixed on the kingdom due to his father’s word, he made the forest-dwelling a festival;
he was the subduer of Virādha and Rāvaṇa, whose home was the Citrakūṭa mountain,
and who performed deeds in the Daṇḍaka forest that were brought to an end by the curse of the twice-born.
The slayer of fourteen thousand fierce rākṣasas, the ender of Khara,
the pacifier of Triśiras’s life-force, the defiler of the wicked Dūṣaṇa,
the crusher of Mārīca in disguise, and the remover of Janakī’s suffering in separation.
He performed the funeral rites for Jaṭāyu, was skilled in the slaying of Kabandha,
dwelt in the cave of Ṛṣyamūka, formed a friendship with the five monkeys,
and cast the bones of Dundubhi upon the great mountain with the tip of his left foot.
He who split the seven palm trees that were difficult to pierce due to their thorns;
the slayer of Vālin, the lord of Kiṣkindhā; the bestower of the kingdom upon his friend Sugrīva;
and he for whom the great city of Laṅkā was consumed by the fire from the tail of Añjaneya’s own offspring.
He who agitated the ocean with the clearly manifest fury of his separation from Sītā;
who constructed a marvelous bridge over the sea by tossing up mountain peaks;
and who dispelled the fear of Vibhīṣaṇa, who was terrified by the blow of his foot.
He who conquered the terrifying army of Rāvaṇa, which had been provoked by the words of Aṅgada;
he who slew the heroes Nikumbha, Kumbha, Dhūmrākṣa, Kumbhakarṇa, and others;
and he who, intoxicated by his power, removed the heads of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa after he had withstood Mount Kailāsa.
Eager to conceal Sītā, who had been purified by contact with fire;
having obtained his own refuge—the kingdom—through the bodies of the monkey and the king of the rākṣasas;
the sovereign of Ayodhyā, the crest-jewel of the entire host of kṣatriyas.
The king, whose deeds are inconceivable, has attained the rise of the lion-throne;
