he is the crusher of the wicked and the evil-minded, the sole protector of the lowly and the destitute,
the generator of all prosperity, and the discernor of the path for animals.
He whose sole means of livelihood was the son of a brahmin scorched by the fierce asceticism of a śūdra;
whose heart was afflicted by wicked speech; the one who caused the exile of Sītā;
the performer of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha); and the father of the illustrious Kuśa and Lava.
He who had abandoned his brother Lakṣmaṇa for the sake of truth, who skillfully gathered the people under his care,
whose fame was like a beautiful ear-ornament, and who destroyed the thick darkness with the light of his renown;
Bharata, who renounced the royal throne at the lotus-feet of his elder brother.
Endowed with all excellent qualities, he is the destroyer of ten million gandharvas;
Lakṣmaṇa is devoted to his elder brother and the ender of the hosts of the gods' enemies;
he is the taker of Indrajit’s life, possessed of brothers, and one who has abandoned strife.
Śatrughna, the subduer of enemies, the bringer of Lavaṇa’s end,
praised by his noble brothers, a mine of virtues lauded by the virtuous;
Śrīmukunda, the refuge of all, who dwells within the hollow of a banyan leaf.
The bird who placed the entire world upon his slender belly, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu;
the primordial leader of the hosts of gods, who is fond of measured praise and prostrations;
the one who accomplished the secret mantras of the gods terrified by the fierce body of Vṛtra.
Devoted to Brahman, praising the Brahmins, and affectionate toward those who revere Brahman;
his limbs were moistened by water from cow-prints, and he was the refuge for the Vālakhilya sages.
He brought misfortune to evil-doers, was the best among sacrificers, and caused wonder even to kings.
The performer of many horse sacrifices, the crest-jewel of the liberal,
the son of Vāsava, Vyāsa, the arranger of the Vedic branches,
the teacher of the Purāṇas and the Mahābhārata, he who desires the welfare of the world in its age of turmoil.
The joy of Rohiṇī’s heart, Balabhadra, the refuge of strength, Saṃkarṣaṇa, the plow-handed one, whose weapon is the mace and whose splendor is stainless;
whose body is as white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon; the slayer of Tāla and the destroyer of Dhenuka.
The slayer of Muṣṭika and Ariṣṭa, who dragged the Yamunā with his plow;
the destroyer of Pralamba, the crusher of Rukmī, and the ender of Dvivida;
the one who gladdens Revatī, the lover of Rāmā, and the ender of Balvala.
The uprooter of Hastināpura, whose excellent feet are honored by the Kauravas;
he whose lotus-feet are praised by Brahmā and the other gods, the protector of the divine Yādavas;
the Lord of Māyā, the Great Illusionist, who ordains the Great Illusion.
The full moon in the ocean of the Yadu lineage, the younger brother beloved by Baladeva;
the Supreme Brahman in human form, perfectly complete and of supreme manifestation;
filled with all knowledge and other perfections, he is the ancient one of perfect bliss.
Clad in yellow garments, with a yellow sleep, and possessing great ascetic power within his yellow abode;
broad-chested and long-armed, adorned with precious jeweled earrings;
he is graced by a golden crown and garlands upon his shimmering cheeks.

With beautiful ears and brilliantly shining earrings shaped like sea-monsters, with dark, curly, and very glossy locks of hair, he has a face like the full moon; he possesses a fine nose, jasmine-like teeth,
and radiant lips like red lotuses.
With a gentle smile, gazing with beautiful arched brows,
possessing a neck like a conch shell, and large Brahma-like [forehead], he was adorned with bracelets and armlets;
wearing the Kaustubha gem and a forest garland, he bore the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
His limbs were marked by the auspicious Śrīvatsa, and he was endowed with all the primary and secondary marks. He had a flat belly and a deep navel; he was irreproachable and independent.
His hips were adorned with a girdle of tinkling bells that clung to his rounded form.
His pair of shanks and knees are symmetrical, and he is adorned with exquisite and beautiful splendor;
his lotus-feet are marked with the signs of a banner, a thunderbolt, a goad, and a lotus and arrow;
the nectar of his lotus-feet is drunk by the swarms of bees that are his devotees.
His great mind is illuminated by the moonlight of the moonstones that are his nails;
he is adorned by the shimmering anklets placed upon his pair of lotus-feet;
and he is the expansive, radiant lotus within the sky of the hearts of his devotees.
The joy of all living beings, beloved by the praises of Vasudeva,
the delight of Devakī, the bringer of bliss to the world, and the dispeller of the fear of his devotees; he who follows Śeṣa, who reclines upon Śeṣa, and who bestows honor and joy upon Yaśodā.
He who brings joy to Nanda, the kinsman of the cowherds, cowherd-women, and the community of Gokula;
he who gladdens all the people of Vraja, the beloved of his devotees, and the lover of cows;
he whose limbs are beautiful with auspicious marks, and who stands between the arms of the cowherd women.
He who suckles the breast of Pītapūtanikā, who dries up the life-force of Pūtanā,
who dwells upon the chest of Pūtanā, and who bestows liberation upon Pūtanā;
he who brings joy to the assembled people and who causes the overturning of the cart.
The Lord of Wisdom who has received the blessings of the Brahmins, the locus of qualities such as minuteness (laghimā),
the grasper of Tṛṇāvarta’s throat, the destroyer of Tṛṇāvarta,
the producer of joy for his mother, and he who beholds the universe from within his mother’s womb.
Delighting in children's play, finding joy in the sports and speech of children,
he brings pleasure to the cowherds and cowherdesses, imitating their songs and dances;
his limbs are smeared with fresh butter, and he is fond of bits of fresh butter.
He who partakes of a morsel of fresh butter, yet is no thief of the butter;
Dāmodara, the uprooter of Arjuna, the one who brings joy to the sole mind of the cowherd;
he who sports in the forest of Vṛndāvana and is skilled in manifold pastimes.
The drawer of Vatsa’s tail, the slayer of the demon Vatsāsura,
the enemy of Baka, the destroyer of sins, and the annihilator of Death for children;
he who is fond of the beautifully cleansed sandbanks frequented by the breezes of the Yamunā.

Abiding among the multitude of cowherd boys, he partakes of the food of smooth curds and rice; he acts for the pleasure of the cows, the cowherds, and the cowherd girls; he is the sustainer of wealth and the shatterer of delusion. He is the creator of delusion for the Ordainer (Brahmā) and the exhibitor of most marvelous sovereignty.
He whose lotus feet are praised by Brahmā, who shattered the intellect of the cowherd boys,
who crushed the pride of Kālīya, and who is fond of the praises of the serpent women;
he who extinguished the forest fire, the sustainer of the entire Vraja community, and the life of all people.
He who dispels the forest fire of hardship upon entering the Muñja forest;
he whose play brings happiness at all times; he who is adorned with a crest of peacock feathers;
he who is the life-breath of the cowherd women; and he who is skilled in the playing of the flute.
He who obstructed the concealment of the gopīs, who bestowed the boon of the gopīs' vow,
who quelled the pride of the brahmins, and who granted grace to the wives of the brahmins;
he who destroyed the excellence of Indra’s hundred sacrifices and removed the arrogance and intoxication of Śakra.
He who upheld Mount Govardhana, who grants fearlessness to the people of Vraja; whose glorious fame rivals that of Indra, the cowherd (Govinda) who is the festival of Gokula;
the protector of Nanda, whose virtuous stories are praised by the god Varuṇa.
Praised by the inhabitants of Vraja, He reveals His own realm;

He brings delight to the gopīs who are intoxicated with passion by the sound of His beautiful flute. He humbles the pride of the wives of the cowherds and holds festivals for the celebration of His own glory.
He who delights the women of Vraja, the beloved of the beautiful maidens of Vraja;
he who rejoices in the Rāsa-dance, the ornament of the great circle of the Rāsa;
he who brings fragrance to the forest of Vṛndāvana, and performs his pastimes on the banks of the Yamunā.
He who was sung in the songs of the cowherd girls; he who severed the head of Śaṅkhacūḍa;
he who liberated the terrified Nanda from being swallowed by the mouth of the great serpent;
he whose feet are worshipped by Sudarśana; and he who is the destroyer of wicked misfortunes.
He who has hair as his enemy, the destroyer of the sky, whose fame was proclaimed by Nārada; he who does what is pleasing to Akrūra, the slayer of the cruel dyer, and the maker of beautiful attire;
he who is enriched by the garland given by Sudāman, and who was anointed with sandalwood paste by the hunchbacked woman.
He who brings joy to the people of Mathurā, who shattered the fierce bow, who utterly destroyed Kaṃsa’s army, who is honored by hosts of merchants and Brahmins,
who slew the great elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, and who crushed Cāṇūra.
He who held a boundless festival for men and women gathered in the hall of passion;
he who brought about the destruction of Kaṃsa and granted his sister the attainment of a form like his own;
he who made King Ugrasena his father and brought happiness to all beings.
He who brings joy to his father and mother, who bestows grace upon the cowherd Nanda,
who took Sāndīpani as his teacher and crossed to the further shore of the ocean of knowledge;
he who destroyed the Daitya Pañcajana and is fond of the conch Pāñcajanya.
He who restored the deceased child to Sāndīpani, who is honored by Kāla and Yama; who pacified the fever of desire in the Sairandhrī, who bestowed joy upon Akrūra;
who bears the Śārṅga bow, and who is skilled in the fitting of various arrows.
Clad in an impenetrable divine armor, with the illustrious Dāruka as his charioteer,
he has a banner marked by the king of birds, holds the discus in his hand, and wields the mace;
he is enriched by the sword Nandaka and possesses an inexhaustible quiver of arrows.
Unconquerable in battle by gods or asuras, he is the conqueror of the Magadhan hosts;
he is the destroyer of the Magadhan army and the protector of the city of Mathurā.
He is the builder of the city of Dvārakā and the regulator of the stability of the world.
He is the generator of all prosperity, the bringer of joy to his own kin,
the earth that is not scorched by the wish-fulfilling tree, and the one who brought the ground of the Sudharma assembly hall.
He is the destroyer of the Yavana demon and the fulfiller of Mucukunda’s desires.
He whose chariot departed for Kuṇḍina after consultation with Rukmiṇī and the twice-born;
the snatcher of Rukmiṇī’s necklace; the one who caused the shaving of Rukmin’s head;
the doer of what is dear to Rukmiṇī; the manifest husband of the beautiful Rukmiṇī.
He is the honeybee drinking from the lotus-face of Rukmiṇī;
he is the pure one who conquered the Lord of the Bears (Jāmbavat) for the sake of the Syamantaka jewel out of devotion to himself;
his lotus-feet were worshipped by Jāmbavat; and he is the manifest husband of Jāmbavatī.
He who took Satyabhāmā by the hand, the beloved of the beautiful Kālindī;
he who conquered seven bulls with sharp horns and shattered the herds of kings;
the supreme leader whose consort is Satyā, the daughter of Nagnajit.
Lord of Bhadrā, beloved of Lakṣmaṇā, Lord of the beloved Mitravindā;
conqueror of Mura, destroyer of the army of Pīṭha, slayer of Naraka;
he whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the Earth, remover of the fear of Bhagadatta.
The leader who brought forth divine women and jewels from the hells;
he who enjoyed the amorous dalliances of one hundred and eight, and two thousand eight hundred women;
and he who, through the words of Satyabhāmā and Balarāma, carried away the Pārijāta tree.

Born from the power of the Lord of Gods, possessing various pleasures born of his wife, he humbled the pride of Rukmiṇī; yet, though he was the father of Kāma and the son of Sāmba, he remained uninfatuated by the charms of women, and possessed countless sons and grandsons.
He who severed the arms of Bāṇa—the grandson of Uśanas—along with his six arrows; he who destroyed the Pramathas led by Nandin; he who effortlessly conquered Maheśvara;
he whose feet were praised by Mahādeva; and he who liberated King Nṛga from suffering.
He who protects his own people from the affliction of those who seize the property of Brahmins;

the slayer of Pauṇḍraka and the one who took the head of the King of Kāśī; the eternally unconquered; he who is propitiated by the vow of Sudakṣiṇā; and the destroyer of Śiva’s magical rites with fire.
The burner of Vārāṇasī, whose majesty was displayed by Nārada;
he of wondrous sovereignty and greatness, the promoter of all dharmas;
and he for whom virtuous stories were told by kings distressed by the destruction of Jarāsaṃdha.
He accomplishes the weighty tasks of true friends as directed by Nārada;
he follows his wife, children, true friends, those of virtuous conduct, and the company of the noble;
he undertakes the effort to slay Jarāsaṃdha and bestows happiness upon the lord of the earth.
He who performs the duties of a true friend, who inaugurates the Rājasūya sacrifice,
who is praised by all the hosts of ṛṣis, who took the life of the King of Cedi,
who is honored by the people of Indraprastha, and who bewildered Duryodhana.

The destroyer of the city of Maheśadattasaubhāgya, the slayer of enemies, the cutter-off of Dantavakra’s foes, and the bestower of the final destination upon Dantavakra; the crusher of Vidūratha and the one who removes the heavy burden of the earth.
The messenger of Pārtha, the benefactor of Pārtha, the purpose of Pārtha, and the charioteer of Pārtha;
the eradicator of Pārtha’s delusion, the revealer of the Gītā scripture,
and the bestower of the state of heroic liberation upon the life-breath that had entered Pārtha’s arrow.
He is the burner of the wicked, such as Duryodhana; the giver of liberation to Bhīṣma;
the one who took away the horse for Arjuna’s Aśvamedha sacrifice; the establisher of Arjuna’s kingdom;
the bestower of Pṛthā’s desired boon; the giver of victory to Bhīma; and the giver of victory itself.
The bestower of desired gifts to Yudhiṣṭhira, the one who brought joy to Draupadī;
he whose feet were moved by Sahadeva, whose body was honored by Nakula;
the one who restored the Pūru lineage whose embryos had been consumed by the Brahmāstra.
The festival of the women of the city of the Paurava king’s arrival at Dvārakā was proclaimed as a great event by the inhabitants of the Ānarta country;
it brought joy to beloved ones and shattered the poverty of friends and brahmins.
He who acts for the benefit of his dear friends under the guise of visiting sacred sites, the delighter of Nanda,
the bestower of knowledge upon the cowherd women, he who celebrated the festival of his father’s sacrifice,
the speaker of righteous conduct, the performer of righteous conduct, and the protector of righteous conduct.
The giver of the knowledge of the Self to his father, the restorer of the dead son to Devakī,
the one who did what was pleasing to Śrutadeva, the increaser of the joy of the people of Mithilā,
the subduer of Arjuna’s pride, and the giver of a dead Brahmin’s son.
He who brings satisfaction to the multitude of jewel-like women, whose festival is the play of human amorous sport;
who gladdens beings like ten million moons, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns;
whom ten million Deaths cannot overcome, and who is more enchanting than ten million Kāmas.
Possessing the wealth of ten million Yakṣa kings, possessing the prowess of ten million Maruts,
as deep as ten million oceans, and as unshakable as ten million Himalayas;
he is the remover of the sins of ten million horse-sacrifices and possesses a name superior to ten million sacred fords.
He is the destroyer of death for ten million nectars, the granter of desires for ten million wish-fulfilling cows;
he is enriched by the splendor of ten million Indras and is the leader of ten million Brahmā-eggs.
His every effort is unfailing, his fame is infinite, and his prowess is boundless.
He is renowned for granting all desired objects; his name is meritorious to hear and to chant;
he is praised in song by Brahmā and the other gods, and his conduct transcends that of mortals.
He is without beginning, middle, or end, and is devoid of increase or decrease.
The sole bestower of knowledge to his devotees, headed by Uddhava, he is the embodiment of wisdom;
he whose fierce prowess destroyed the Yadu lineage under the pretext of the Brahmins' curse,
who grants heaven even while in the body to those afflicted by old age and disease, and who is praised by the dwellers of heaven.
His glory brings joy to those seeking liberation, to the liberated, and to worldly people;
his fame destroys the impurities of the Kali age and is auspicious to hear.
He is dear to his devotees, beneficial to his devotees, and a lotus for the bees that are his devotees.
The protector of all upon being merely remembered, the shatterer of machines and mantras;
he whose name bestows all prosperity, who is fond of garlands of *tulasī*;
he of immeasurable form, with radiant and priceless ornaments upon his limbs.
He who grants the sole happiness of the universe, the protector of the joy of all virtuous people,
the crest-jewel upon the heads of all the gods, possessing wondrous and infinite enjoyments;
Adhokṣaja, the sustainer of living beings, the refuge of all holy men.
His name shatters all fears; he is the destroyer of suffering as soon as he is remembered.
He delights the people with the joy of hearing his own glory; he is an ocean of virtues.
His form is indescribable; he is the refuge for those who suffer and the life of all living beings.
The ultimate reality, the supreme object of knowledge, the supreme light, the supreme goal;
the Blessed One, who is to be known through the Vedānta, an ocean of infinite bliss;
whose fame lies in destroying the bonds of the world, and who is the refuge for all living beings in the universe.
The sole lord of the Vaikuṇṭha realm, beloved by the people of Vaikuṇṭha;
Pradyumna, the son of Rukmiṇī, the slayer of Śambara, and the lover of Rati;
the one with the flower-bow, the conqueror of the universe, the radiant one, and the destroyer of the life-force [of his enemies].
Aniruddha, the son of Kāma, whose source is sound, the one of great stride;
the husband of Uṣā, the lord of the Vṛṣṇis, Hṛṣīkeśa, the lord of the mind;
the teacher of the glorious Bhāgavata, the ocean of all Vedānta.
Śuka, the knower of all dharmas, honored by King Parīkṣit;
the illustrious Buddha, the destroyer of evil intellects, who excluded the Daityas from the Vedas;
the proclaimer of the path of heresy, the conqueror of the world without weapons.
Kalkī shall be the shrouder of the Kali age and the restorer of the Satya age;
he will be the son of Vipra Viṣṇuyaśas and the promoter of the lost Dharma.
He will be Sārasvata, a sovereign ruler, and a powerful conqueror of the three worlds.
The speaker of the true Dharma during the eighth intermediate period, beloved of Vairocana;
Āpakara, the Lord of Ramā, the destroyer of the host of the enemies of the immortals;
Śrutendra, the benefactor of those who act for the welfare [of others], the bestower of steadfastness, heroism, liberation, and strength.
Viṣvaksena, the friend of Śambhu, the protector of the tenth interval,
the benefactor to the ocean-like lineage of Brahma-Sāvarṇi, the increaser of the universe; the bridge of dharma, the destroyer of unrighteousness, the bestower of the state of the Vaidhya-tantra.
The destroyer of the Asuras, the son of Devārthaka, the one of excellent speech; he whose splendor is self-sustained, the son of Sūnṛtā, whose brilliance is truth, the son of a twice-born;
the protector of the Manu-yuga against enemies, the shatterer of the cities of the netherworlds.
The divine Hotṛ, the one whose essence is the Bṛhatī meter, the Lord of Heaven, the most beloved;
the protector within the thirteen internal spaces, the Lord of the community of yogis and yoginīs;
the performer of the sacrificial session, the long-armed one, the son of Vinatā, the supreme knower.
He who proclaims the ritual section alone, the founder of the Vedic systems,
the Supreme Lord, the eldest of the gods, Brahmā, the lord of the creators of the universe,
born from the lotus, whose vehicle is the swan, the grandfather of all the worlds.
Viṣṇu is the protector of the entire world, peaceful, pure, and eternal;
he is worthy of worship by the twice-born, an ocean of compassion, the refuge, and affectionate toward his devotees.
Rudra is the deluded one, Śiva is the teacher, Śambhu is the destroyer of all, and Hara is the one who takes away.
Kapardin, Śaṃkara, the wielder of the trident, the three-eyed, the impenetrable Maheśvara;
the overseer of all, possessed of all powers, the object of all, facing in all directions;
the abode of all, the form of all, the cause of all causes.
Thus, O Brahmin, has this Thousand Names of Viṣṇu been told;
it pacifies all sins and bestows the fruit of all desired objects.
It quickly purifies the mind and increases devotion to the Blessed Lord.
It removes all obstacles, bestows all wonders and sovereign powers,
pacifies all suffering, and grants the fruits of the four aims of human life—
through hearing, reciting, and chanting it with supreme faith and devotion.
Reciting this daily, a twice-born man among all castes whose soul is devoted to the feet of Viṣṇu shall obtain learning; a Kṣatriya, this entire earth;
a Vaiśya, a great treasure; and a Śūdra, his desired success.
If one should commit thirty-two offenses against Hari, whether knowingly or unknowingly,
or if one should commit ten offenses against the Name through negligence,
one should indeed recite this with a concentrated mind, cause it to be heard, or chant it.
Whether one remembers them or even hears of them, one is immediately liberated from those [fetters];
there exists nothing more meritorious than this in the three worlds,
by the mere recitation of which one is released from the bondage of existence.
Therefore, you should constantly perform the recitation with devotion and faith;
this Thousand Names of Viṣṇu is the cause of the Lord’s pleasure.
Śrī Nārada said:
I am blessed and I am graced by you, whose nature is supreme compassion,
since the thousand supreme names of Kṛṣṇa have been proclaimed.
Even if, due to laziness or negligence, one is unable to recite them all every day—
"O Lord, I am unable [to do that]; tell me, O Master, what should I do?
Śrī Śiva said:
"O twice-born one, if you are not able to recite it all every day,"

Then, O brahmin-sage, say "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" every day; by this alone, everything is accomplished for you at once. How much more so, then, from the recitation of the thousand names of the Blessed One?
I take refuge in that Kṛṣṇa in the form of a cowherd, by the mere chanting of whose name a person truly crosses the ocean of worldly existence. (Sātvatatantra 6.225)
The Seventh Chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
"Those who indeed listen daily to the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu..."
Or else, O Brahmin,

those who take refuge in the lotus feet of Viṣṇu, out of devotion and by their own choice, may recite or remember [the names] with reverence— whether a hundred, twenty, ten, five, or even just one, O twice-born one.
O Nārada, I see no end to the merit of their fruit,
since by them the Blessed One himself— Supreme Bliss and the Master— has been won over;
for his very name is indeed the supreme sacred ford and the merit-bestowing field.
Name alone is the supreme deity; name alone is the supreme austerity.
Name alone is the supreme gift; name alone is the supreme ritual act.
Name alone is the supreme dharma; name alone is proclaimed to be the supreme wealth.

O best of the twice-born, for devotees, the Name alone is desire, and the Name alone is liberation; and for those who possess desire, the Name alone is the means of accomplishment. The Name alone is supreme devotion, and the Name alone is the supreme goal.
The Name alone is the supreme object of recitation; the Name alone is the supreme prayer. For those free from desire, the Name is wealth, providing the fruits of liberation and enjoyment.
The Name is the highest happiness; the Name alone is the cause of dispassion.
The name is known as that which purifies the *sattva* and bestows knowledge;
it is the state of liberation for those seeking release, and the granter of all desires for those who possess longing.
It is the fruit for the Vaiṣṇavas; therefore, one should always remember the Name.

The name of the Blessed One is proclaimed as the remover of all sins when remembered, even when uttered through convention, jesting, negligence, or the fever of affliction. Whatever power exists for the eradication of sin resides within the name of Hari.

Indeed, as long as a sinful person does not chant the name of Hari, whether knowingly or unknowingly, he is unable to commit sin at all; for the chanting of Hari’s name quickly burns away a mass of sins, just as fire consumes cotton.
O best of the twice-born, when the name of Hari is indeed proclaimed with faith by a person, it bestows upon him the fruit of truth in due course:
the destruction of sin, great merit, and the fourfold dispassion.

From that [guru], one shall immediately obtain service to the guru, self-realization, the destruction of delusion, and the realization of perfect bliss; therein, one shall attain stability. Śrī Nārada said:
"O best of gods, you have described fourfold detachment;
explain this for the benefit of the world as the cause of knowledge.
Śrī Śiva said:
O best of the twice-born, when a person enjoys sense objects free from attachment, that is proclaimed as *amāna*.
Even when the object of enjoyment is devoid of sweetness, one maintains one's livelihood [without craving].
Know that, O best of beings, the second is called "separation" (vyatireka).
When there is an absence of joy in the mind, enjoyment is experienced by the senses alone;
this third [state] is proclaimed by men as being called the "senses" (indriya).
O Brahmin, the absence of passion in both the mind and the senses, as well as the withdrawal from sense objects, is proclaimed as the fourth; this supreme state,
O best of the twice-born, arises swiftly.

And that supreme, pure knowledge bestows the bliss of Brahman. O Brahmin, that supreme state of Viṣṇu is not attained through sacred fords, gifts, austerities, fire-offerings, castes, vows, fasts, or various types of yoga.
O Brahmin, dear to Hari, by the mere chanting of His name, men do not fall; they surely attain [liberation], of this there is no doubt—
even one joined with great sins, by chanting the name of the Teacher of the World.

He certainly crosses over, there is no doubt; I speak the truth itself. O Brahmin, having abandoned even the impurity of the Kali age and all sinful deeds, he who is devoted to nothing other than the Name goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, by the mere name alone, a person indeed crosses the ocean of existence;
there is no doubt in this, provided there is no offense against the Name.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, a man who desires his own welfare should apply himself with effort to it.
"One should never, under any circumstances, commit the ten offenses against the name of Viṣṇu.
Śrī Nārada said:
"I have heard from the mouth of the Blessed One regarding the twenty-two offenses."
"O Lord, describe to us these ten [offenses] by the name of Viṣṇu.
Śrī Śiva said:
"Listen, O Nārada; I shall indeed speak of the offenses against Viṣṇu."
O Sage, by performing these acts, men constantly go to hell:
touching Viṣṇu without having bathed; bathing [an image] without using a conch shell;
touching him while in a state of ritual impurity; or drinking the water from his feet after he has eaten.
Worship without sound, worship without the offering of food (naivedya),
worship performed while seated on a high throne, fanning with a fan during the cold, seeing a woman in her courses, and placing the bell upon the ground.
In the month of Pauṣa, there is the touch of sandalwood, and likewise, in the summer, there is no such touch.
There is the contact of flowers with water, a great festival without fire-offerings (homa),
and having performed worship, one sees [the deity] from behind and likewise circumambulates in front.
Eating food at the door of the Blessed One, feeling dejection,
putting on wooden sandals in the house of Viṣṇu, and wearing a woolen blanket;
entering with the left foot first, jumping about, and eating cooked food [are all forbidden].
Spitting phlegm, cleaning one's teeth with grass,
mounting a vehicle in the presence of the deity, regarding the offering as a mere material object,
and addressing the Śālagrāma stone as "stone" or the fixed image as "image"— [these are all offenses].
Not praising the glory of Hari, treating a Vaiṣṇava as equal to an ordinary man,
regarding Viṣṇu as equal to other deities, and offering oblations intended for another—
these are the thirty-two offenses against the names of Viṣṇu; now hear [of the offenses] against the names.
By the name of the virtuous, there is contempt for the teachers of distinction regarding Śiva and Viṣṇu;

there is reviling of the Veda, dispute over names, evil intent despite the thousandfold repetition of the Name, the notion of equality between the Name and other dharmas, and giving devoid of faith. (SatvT 7.38–39)

O best of the twice-born, even after hearing [the names], a lack of faith and the notion of "I" (egoism) regarding the chanting— these, indeed, are the offenses concerning the names that I have declared;
they must be avoided with effort by men, since they are the causes of hell.
Śrī Nārada said:
O Lord, for ordinary men whose minds are attached to sense objects,
offenses against Hari do not indeed cease to exist quickly.
"Therefore, O Lord, you ought to explain to me the manner by which even ordinary people cross over the transgressions they have committed. Śrī Śiva said:
Having performed a hundred circumambulations, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff;

Keśava forgives a hundred offenses of his own for such a person. He who performs a single circumambulation but does not bow with his knees and head [to the ground]— [his offense is likewise forgiven].
That [offering] of his would be fruitless; therefore, one should bow down to each [deity].
If they should utter your name, "Lord of the World," you will forgive their hundred offenses; of this there is no doubt.
One crosses over the offenses against the Name by the constant chanting of the Name itself;
except for an offense committed against a devotee,
one who takes refuge at the lotus feet of Viṣṇu crosses over all offenses, even when deprived of His grace.
"Indeed, one may cross over even the offenses against Viṣṇu by the chanting of His names.
There is no other remedy for offenses against the devotees of Viṣṇu.
Śrī Nārada said:
"Tell me of the offenses of devotees so that there may be a remedy for them,
O Blessed One, for the sake of favoring the worlds and for my own as well.
Śrī Śiva said:
O best of the twice-born, seizing all the possessions of a devotee of Viṣṇu,
reviling a supreme devotee, and even striking one in a dream—
these are offenses against devotees; hear now the remedy for them.
Having given back that wealth doubled and having performed prostrations at his feet, one should say,
"Forgive me for that fault which was a plundering of wealth.
One should remain concentrated for as many months as it took to perform that scolding.
Free from envy, one should attend upon him; through his grace, one is purified.
One should serve him tirelessly for as long as one lives;
through his grace alone, there shall be atonement for those sins, and not otherwise.
Without performing these expiations for these [sins], there is no liberation from hell.
O Brahmin, that which was committed through ignorance is destroyed by their grace;
however, one should perform double the penance if done knowingly—this is the eternal Dharma.
In the case of a son, a disciple, or a wife, there is no fault in instructing them;
however, if it is done by another [than these], a transgression certainly occurs—of this there is no doubt.
[This applies even when] pulling the hair, striking with the foot, or slapping the face.
I see no atonement for that; therefore, one should not practice those [acts]. (SatvT 7.57, Sātvatatantra, eighth chapter)
Śrī Śiva said:
Now I shall declare to you this supreme secret, by which, indeed, through abiding with faith in Hari, devotion becomes firm. (SatvT 8.1)
One should place trust in the Lord, in the sacred ford, and in the Dharma, because they carry one across suffering;
having abandoned that [trust in worldly things], one should joyfully take refuge at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.
"The Lord of the World, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, is my refuge."
With a concentrated mind, one should utter this [mantra] before that deity and before one's own guru.
O twice-born, having abandoned the worship of other deities through offerings of oblations and the like,
one should worship Kṛṣṇa alone— who embodies all gods— with such an understanding.
A householder who is a devotee of Viṣṇu should perform the daily, occasional, and necessary rites while remembering Kṛṣṇa with his mind. Furthermore,
regarding these [rites], whatever worship of other deities is prescribed according to the rules—
She too should be worshipped after the worship of Kṛṣṇa, while remembering Him in the heart.
On other occasions, one should not remember the separate worship of other deities;
likewise, one should never perform rites for specific desires or those that are prohibited.
Having abandoned wife, son, friends, and the like, those who have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa and are devoted to the glorification of Hari— for them, no further duty remains.
O twice-born one, having performed the worship of other deities with desire, [one should offer] a bali-oblation.
One who has fallen away from devotion quickly [perishes] and does not turn back from cyclic existence.
One whose soul is possessed by desire and who is devoid of compassion, performing the slaughter of animals,
is cooked in hell for as many years as there are hairs on the animal.
There is no fault whatsoever in the scriptural injunction regarding the immolation of an animal in sacrifice;
yet, even for those possessed by passion, engagement in such acts is inferior, while renunciation is superior.
Having performed worship to other deities and having abandoned the sacrificial animal, those lowest of men—
"If they go to heaven, then who goes to hell?
'He will eat me again, whose meat I give'—
thus indeed do the wise explain the etymology of the word 'meat' (māṃsa)."

One who, while relying on devotion to Viṣṇu, practices the slaughter of animals or performs the worship of other deities, certainly falls away from grace. Those living beings who, having attained human birth, do not worship the feet of Hari [are likewise lost].
They are to be pitied if they have no refuge even in stationary beings and the like.
I, Brahmā, and the lords of the gods worship him day and night;
therefore, who is a greater deity than Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person?
He whose grace all the worlds, together with their guardians, await,
and whom even Lakṣmī herself serves with devotion—
what god could be superior to that Janārdana, the beloved of Lakṣmī?
Into whose name do men not enter the supreme state?
Since the worship of his feet is the root of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,
what god is greater than that high-souled one, the ocean of compassion?

Who is a greater deity than the Teacher of the World, who is so easy to propitiate, that one who always honors him even with a mere trifle is considered superior? Whatever person worships him with whatever disposition whatsoever— SatvT_8.20—
One attains the desired accomplishment as well as liberation, which is free from fear from any quarter.
Who, then, is a greater deity than the son of Devakī, the delighter of the gods,
who descended and spread his fame for the sake of the world’s liberation?
Therefore, having abandoned the worship of other deities,
one should, through the instruction of a true guru, honor the two feet of Kṛṣṇa by means of the offering of bali;
and one should daily hear the supreme, auspicious glory of Viṣṇu.
One should utter the name with the mouth alone and remember it with the mind.
One should indeed show affection toward the devotees of Viṣṇu and avoid those who are not devotees.
Eating what is obtained by chance, one should not exert excessive effort for the sake of pleasure.
One should dwell in houses like a guest, provided one does not cause them any distress;
if one must cause them distress, one should dwell separately among those devoted to Viṣṇu.
This applies whether one is a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic.
Without the association of Vaiṣṇavas, a person shall never attain perfection.
Without the company of devotees, devotion does not arise in anyone;
without devotion, there is neither detachment nor knowledge, and one does not enjoy liberation.
Therefore, having abandoned even the external marks of the stages of life (āśrama), one should dwell together with devotees,
for through association with them devotion to Hari arises, surpassing both Vedic study and fame. O Nārada, even for a mere moment’s association with a devotee of Viṣṇu, [the result is immeasurable].
Heaven and liberation are not equal, much less other pleasures and the like.
Therefore, with effort, a person should cultivate association with the followers of Hari;
since even animals obtain liberation through this, how much more so humans?
By association with them alone, a person certainly attains Viṣṇu,
even without detachment and knowledge, because Viṣṇu is present near them.
By associating with those [devotees], a human being hears of the association with Hari even once.
If he is unable to renounce it, he may become like a pleasant river;
even one who does not know its flavor, if he somehow comes into contact with it,
becomes a knower of its flavor and, becoming great, is liberated from the bondage of karma.
Then, devoted to that dharma within the stainless self of the Blessed One,
he attains supreme devotion which grants all desires. Having recognized this devotion, no person whatsoever would desire liberation [any longer].
O twice-born one, what need is there to mention the state of *sālokya* and other such goals, or any other happiness?
O best of the twice-born, devotees of Viṣṇu attain liberation even without [seeking] such fruits;
for that very reason, they know nothing else superior to that which consists of bliss.
Since Hari always dwells in their hearts as if inscribed there, He—
the embodiment of supreme bliss— is bound to them by the creeper of love. (Sātvatatantra 8.38)
The Ninth Chapter.
Śrī Nārada said:
"O Lord of Gods, such is the merit found in serving the feet of the Blessed One."
"From where do human beings worship another deity? By what desire?
Śrī Śiva said:
"O best of Brahmins, in the primordial truth (ādisatya), men were devoted solely to Viṣṇu."

They do not worship any other deity whatsoever without Viṣṇu. O twice-born one, for the sake of attaining self-worship, we indeed worship Hṛṣīkeśa— who consists of all the gods— with body, speech, and mind.
Then the all-pervading Lord, the God of gods, the Lord of Ramā, being pleased, said:
"Having descended, I shall perform sacrifice for you while causing the worlds to sacrifice as well.
Then all people, with concentrated minds, will sacrifice to you."
"By this, worship shall be brought to you, bringing happiness.
And I was addressed separately by that Brahmin Śrīnivāsa:
"O Maheśvara, always protect me according to the composed Āgamas."

"O Bhadra, you shall always recite this supreme thousand names which remove the sin of contempt for me; this has been requested by me once again. Therefore, having concealed Kṛṣṇa with my scriptures, the deities shall not [be seen]."

O twice-born one, through mechanical devices, mantras, and tantras, [these deities] have been shown to grant results. By means of those scriptures, those of dull intellect, having abandoned Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the world,
constantly worship other deities with offerings of oblations.
Having propitiated various gods out of a desire for the pleasures of diverse sensual objects,
they go at the end of their enjoyments to a hell consisting of their own darkness.
Having seen such worlds, his mind became apprehensive of sin.

"O twice-born one, I went for refuge at the feet of Vāsudeva. With my mind composed, O Brahmin, I offered praise to Puruṣottama with palms joined in reverence, bowing low with my neck bent in humility."
Oṃ, homage be to Kṛṣṇa, the creator of Vikuṇṭha, the kinsman of living beings who take refuge in the play of Your feet,

whose desires are eternally fulfilled, the cause of the supreme goal, the treasury of the knowledge of discernment, the self-existent one. You alone exist before creation, likewise at the time of dissolution, and at the beginning of the ages, in the presence of the wise.

Homage to You, whose conduct is infinite, who shines forth through various bodies; homage to You, the witness of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), time, latent dispositions (*āśaya*), and karma, who performs the boundless sport of their synthesis;
homage, again and again, to Kṛṣṇa, who assumes diverse forms, who is impartial, and to whom devotion has been rendered.
Those who hear, sing, and proclaim your glory— the purifier of the world and the Lord of the universe—
behold no other for their own happiness than the service of your feet;
for those who, possessing nothing, take refuge at your feet, they nourish that happiness which arises from the Self.
The wise who are superior to them know this in its true essence; yet others, though discerning, have their intellects drawn away by desires.
But I, O Lord, though constantly worshipping Your lotus feet, still possess a separate-mindedness;
desiring to manifest my own self, I am today cutting away the impurity that separates me from You.

"Moreover, O Lord Hari, may Your two lotus feet always be for my complete attainment—that contemplation of which, being favorable to all desires, surely brings success; how much more so its vocal recitation!
Having thus recognized my hymn of praise, the Blessed One, who removes the suffering of those who bow before Him, [acted].

That one devoted to compassion made my form an object of my vision: the eternal Lord of All, the source of mercy, marked by the Goddess of Fortune, served by the best of gods and by devotees; his body like a sapphire of intense bliss, with crowns shining with gold, necklaces, pairs of earrings, armlets, girdles, bracelets, anklets, and gleaming tawny bangles. SatvT_9.20–21
Having seen those lotus feet, I then joyfully placed them in my heart, uttering with my mouth the names "Govinda," "Dāmodara," and "Śrī Kṛṣṇa"—the Lord of the three worlds.
Then, as if a flood of water from a waterfall were pouring from my eyes onto my body, and seeing the faltering of my voice through such joy, the Blessed One, who is dear to his devotees, said to me:
"O best of gods, know me; by my compassion for you, a devotee, I shall grant you your most desired boon: a multitude of associations with my own devotees."
"By your recounting the life of Mallī, all people shall indeed become Vaiṣṇavas;
your wife too shall be one who grants her favor and happiness, and you shall be the foremost of my devotees.
Having said this much, the Blessed One departed for the world beyond the mundane.
And having obtained those boons, O bull among the twice-born, I have achieved my purpose.
From that day forward, Pārvatī, the sovereign of the world,
having become a Vaiṣṇavī through association with me, took leave of me, O Lord of the Gods.
You are a great devotee of the Lord; Kumāra and the other great lords,
Kubera and the other deities, and Nandīśa and my other attendants— all of whom take refuge at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa— asked me these questions individually.

[He recited] discourses that are supremely auspicious and the sole purifiers of all the worlds. Then, O best of the twice-born, while she questioned me with her words and I spoke my own words, this son of mine, Gaṇeśa, wrote them down attentively by my side.
The conversations between me and them became scriptures that were enchanting to the world and truly beneficial to all people;
those listeners brought those tantras down to the surface of the earth.
O best of sages, they will recount this extensively in various places.
You, too, shall proclaim this Tantra called Sātvata, which is dear to the Blessed One,
in the presence of Śaunaka and the others at Naimiṣa.
Śrī Nārada said:
I have heard from the mouth of the Blessed One the supreme Sātvata Tantra;
and having heard therein the prohibition of violence, a doubt has arisen in me.
"For the killing of animals in sacrificial rites is ordained by the Veda;
indeed, those who know the Veda have determined that slaughter in sacrifice is non-slaughter.
O Maheśvara, if that [killing] were prohibited, how could there be ritual action based on the Śruti or the Smṛti?"
It should proceed for the sake of all the world, bestowing fruits both in this life and the next.
Śrī Śiva said:
Action is described as being of two kinds: that which is engaged (pravṛtta) and that which is withdrawn (nivṛtta).
O best of Brahmins, by performing actions prescribed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis for the sake of those desiring objects of desire,
a man who acts without transgression goes to heaven;
when his merit is exhausted, he is born again on the surface of the earth among those characterized by their karma.

Practicing the path of withdrawal, the yogi whose mind has abandoned the desire for enjoyment attains the supreme perfection, from which, once gone, he does not return. Therefore, for one who is devoted to worldly activity and attached to various desires—
The permission granted by Brahmins is shown through six kinds of restrictive rules;
for there is no injunction for violence since permission has been given [for it].
Therefore, the wise have declared that one must desist from violence even in the case of sacrifice.

Non-violence is the supreme dharma for all classes and stages of life from the very beginning; and through right conduct, it shall grant the desired fruits to men. Indeed, those who are especially devoted to Viṣṇu abandon the act of violence.
For the Blessed One quickly becomes pleased with living beings through non-violence. Therefore, the Blessed One, the Lord of all,
is said to have entered into all beings, manifesting in various forms among both the stationary and the moving.
For even by me, violence has been prescribed according to the injunctions in the scriptures;
yet that too is for the sake of accomplishing the fruits of desire for those people who are full of longing.
Indeed, how much less do the devotees of Viṣṇu desire anything from me?
Therefore, even when these [rites] are performed, violence is proclaimed to be blameworthy.
Thus, you should especially abandon rites performed for specific desires and listen instead to the meritorious stories of Kṛṣṇa, which grant the fulfillment of all desired goals in every world.
One should listen to the scripture that has been set forth, so that having heard it, one may become devoted to it;

even when [the formal teaching] has ceased, that which is joined with devotion to Hari is proclaimed as primary. Especially [should one hear] the stories of Kṛṣṇa’s divine play, which are most auspicious for the world.
Proclaim this, O best of the twice-born, and listen to it constantly.
Having abandoned refuge in other deities and especially other forms of worship,
those men who worship the feet of Hari, taking Kṛṣṇa alone as their sole refuge— SatvT_9.46–47.
In this world and the next, they are eternally successful and beloved by the Blessed One;
they attain an uninterrupted mass of supreme bliss.
But those who do not know thus—those who are unpeaceful, deluded, and yet consider themselves wise—[do not].
Desiring happiness, they incessantly sacrifice to the gods by slaughtering animals;
and at the end of their enjoyment of desires, those [gods] will surely cut them down.
Thus, O Brahmin, has this supreme Sātvata Tantra been declared.
Sustaining the devotees of Viṣṇu and bestowing all perfections,
through hearing and chanting this, devotion to Kṛṣṇa indeed arises. For a virtuous person who has obtained such devotion, what else remains to be achieved?

O Brahmin, since it was proclaimed by the Blessed One as increasing devotion to Him, this supreme *Viśvasambhava* has been told in this Tantra; and the incarnations of Śrī Viṣṇu are described according to their divisions into complete portions (*sampūrṇāṃśa*) and partial portions (*kalā*).
The various types of devotion, the distinct characteristics of those divisions,
and how, in accordance with the respective ages, service to Śrī Viṣṇu is the means to liberation;
the thousand names of Viṣṇu and the supreme majesty of those names.
The expiation for offenses against Viṣṇu and his devotees,
the secret essence of all that is essential, the cause of the origin of the Tantra,
and the rules regarding violence and its prohibition— in accordance with your questions— [have been explained].
Whatever name, having entered the root of one's ear, been sought after by speech, or remembered within the consciousnesses,
burns away evil and, because of its pure nature, makes that body manifest as faultless.
Therefore, [salutation] to Janārdana, who is infinite and the source of infinite virtues proclaimed by the Vedas.
Homage, repeated homage to you, the one of great majesty, the stainless one, who has eternally attained the self! SatvT_9.57
